subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the conclusion of the routine business I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely:
That the cessation of steamship services on the 26th instant from Vancouver on the mainland of Canada to Victoria, the capital city of British Columbia, a service that has existed since the admission of British Columbia into confederation, will constitute a calamity in national transportation, endanger the safety of the naval base at Esquimalt, the Pacific drydock and the safety of persons, property and commerce now existing.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The urgent matter of public importance which the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, raises and for which he asks leave to move the adjournment of
66968-9-GOJ
the house to discuss has been mentioned earlier. As I recall the reply of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), it was to the effect that he could find no responsibility, legal or constitutional, resting on the federal government to maintain the service in question. With that answer in mind and the possibility of debate that has existed, my first thought about this motion is that it would scarcely qualify, but I do not wish to decide too hastily. If any hon. member could give me some assistance as to the urgency of debating this matter today, having regard to the fact that there was opportunity to discuss almost any subject matter last Monday and Tuesday, after this issue arose, I would appreciate it. I think it unlikely that I can accept the motion, but I am withholding my judgment for the moment at least.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add one word on your request for assistance as to whether or not this is a motion of urgency. I would submit, sir, that it most certainly is one of urgency, because the declaration of Canadian Pacific Steamships is that service between the cities of Vancouver, Victoria and Seattle is to end on the 25th day of this month, and that notice is being given to lay off 200 employees.
I know that you, sir, do not come from British Columbia, but I also know that you are interested in every part of our country. I can assure you that the maintenance of a steamship service between Vancouver and Victoria is of the utmost importance and significance to the province of British Columbia. It is something which has been in effect for a great many years and although there may-I only say "may", sir

be a question of the legal or constitutional responsibility of the federal government, it is and has always been accepted as a part of the transportation system of Canada, and there was an undertaking under the terms of British Columbia coming into confederation that there would be maintained a complete system of transportation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
If I may interrupt the hon. member, I am not disagreeing that this is an urgent matter but I need to be persuaded that we should interrupt other proceedings now to debate this matter. I admit that it is an urgent matter, particularly to those people concerned locally, but the urgency of debate is the problem I have to deal with

British Columbia Ferry Service because here we have private members' day and bills to be debated in their regular order, and I am asked to suspend that order and allow discussion on this matter, not to arrive at any conclusion but just for the purpose of having a debate. I really do not know that I should do that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may say a word, there is no doubt that the question which has been raised is of great concern to people on the west coast, and naturally no one is more concerned over it than I am as a member from the city of Vancouver. However, in view of the fact that the service is not under the jurisdiction of the federal government or of the board of transport commissioners and really is just the same as a service from A to B anywhere in Canada, I suggest that surely it is not in order to adjourn the house to discuss the question of whether	or	not that service should	be suspended.	If	it can be done	in this case, thenit can be done in the case of any other service by ship between any two ports in Canada. For this reason, Your Honour, I submit	that the motion should	not be
accepted.
Hon.	L. B. Pearson	(Leader	of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, the house will remember that the other day I brought this matter up on the orders of the day and asked the government a question concerning it. At that time the Minister of Transport indicated in his reply that it was not a matter of urgency, in the sense that an alternative service was being provided by which people in Victoria could take a bus to Nanaimo and cross from Nanaimo to Vancouver. But surely, Mr. Speaker, not only is it a matter of urgency

and all the information I have received in the last few days would indicate that it is-but it is also one a discussion of which at this particular time might help to prevent the interruption of this service on February 25.
The minister says this is just an ordinary matter in the sense that it is a dispute about the service from point A to point B, but I suggest it is more than that. I suggest that not only might a discussion of the matter at this time and the stand taken by the government prevent interruption of the service, but there is also the question of whether or not there is a legal obligation on the government to prevent the service being interrupted. That matter has been raised and we have not yet had an authoritative opinion. Therefore I suggest that not only is the question one of urgency but it is one that might be assisted by a discussion

at this time so the service will not be interrupted on February 25.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ordinarily I do not intervene in matters such as this, but in accordance with my responsibility as Prime Minister it is necessary for me on occasion to place before Your Honour the situation as it is. Speaking for the moment of the argument of the Leader of the Opposition that there is a legal responsibility, and I am not for a moment accepting it or entering into any controversy in that connection, then recourse to the courts is the proper course to follow by way of an application for a writ of mandamus. If there is a legal responsibility that is the course to follow. The Minister of Transport says there is neither constitutional nor legal responsibility. Certainly there is no administrative responsibility. I would refer Your Honour to Beauchesne, 4th edition, paragraph 100, which reads as follows:
The definite matter of urgent public importance for the discussion of which a member may ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 must involve the administrative responsibility of the government.
The hon. gentleman is properly exercised over the situation, as are other members from the coast, and I am not indicating in any way that he has not raised a very serious matter. Citation 100 in Beauchesne's fourth edition makes it very clear that administrative responsibility on the part of the government would be the only circumstance under which a motion such as this could be entertained. Whatever the legal situation may be, there is no administrative responsibility. Though I fully realize and understand the point of view of the hon. gentleman, the rules would not permit adjournment for this purpose.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You intervened when there was a strike there.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: In order to keep the record straight may I refer to page 805 of Hansard for February 9, where the Minister of Transport was dealing with this matter of legal and constitutional responsibility. He said he would not wish his statement to be taken as final and categorical, but he expressed a tentative opinion. Perhaps the Minister of Justice, who comes from British Columbia, would be able to give us more than a tentative opinion on this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transpori):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: We have still been unable to find any responsibility whatever for this matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I just want to intervene for one moment in answer to what has been said by the Prime Minister.

He has read from Beauchesne, dealing with the urgency of debate, the point upon which you have asked for assistance. He has urged that in order for the house to adjourn its normal proceedings to deal with a matter of urgent public importance the matter must involve the administrative responsibility of the government; that is what Beauchesne says in his fourth edition.
I say that the British North America Act, clearly and in formal language, places the responsibility for navigation and shipping with the federal government. If the responsibility for navigation and shipping lies with the federal government, then there is a responsibility on the government, unless that responsibility is delegated otherwise. There is a responsibility under the British North America Act, but the minister has stated yesterday and again today that there is no legal responsibility. While I accept the minister's statement because of his person, I do not accept the legal implication of the responsible minister's statement. After all, he is giving a legal opinion. I think the house should be allowed to debate this from an urgency standpoint to ascertain whether or not there is this legal liability, and let the Minister of Justice tell us what the position is from the point of view of any agreement that might have been made between the federal government and British Columbia in so far as the service is concerned.
I say, therefore, that until these two points have been determined it would seem to me that there is urgency of debate, and the motion should be allowed.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I realize this is a question of attempting to determine the urgency of debate. Before we embark upon that, I would submit that-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is all I wish to hear; I think the matter must be determined from that point of view.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
That is quite true, and I am going to argue along that line. As I said, I should like to make a preliminary remark. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works were not dealing with that subject matter at all but were attempting to becloud the issue on jurisdiction and responsibility. We all know that shipping on the west coast comes directly under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport in so far as steamship inspection is concerned. So far as labour matters are concerned, they come within the jurisdiction of the federal government, so administration wise the arguments of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works are not valid.
British Columbia Ferry Service
On Monday last the announcement appeared in the newspapers of British Columbia that the coast steamship service was going to discontinue operating the line between Vancouver island and Victoria. It was on that day that the question was asked on the orders of the day. On Monday we had a supply motion and an amendment, which of course was fairly well confined with regard to the matter it covered and was not disposed of until after 8.15 on Tuesday evening.
Therefore the opportunity for debate was confined to probably an hour on Tuesday evening at the outside, at which time other matters were raised. If the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) and others who have a direct interest in this matter had had an opportunity to raise it, they would have done so. There is no fault to be attached to them. It is just that if they did try to bring this matter up they undoubtedly did not catch the eye of the chair in order to raise it. We have not had a chance to do so. I think in that light we should favourably consider the urgency of debate, this being the first opportunity.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: On that point, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think the Minister of Public Works will find it unnecessary to labour that point when he hears my view. I do not determine this matter entirely on the question of whether or not it is an administrative responsibility of the government. Of course it has been said that it is not, and there is a disposition to argue that point. If it is not, the quotation from Beauchesne seems to be clear. If a private company like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company discontinues its service and it is not a service operated by the government of Canada or a service the operation of which is the responsibility of any government agency or crown corporation, it is not a fit subject for this motion.
However, I prefer to deal with the matter on the basis of urgency of debate. This rule should be invoked only in exceptional cases, as hon. members will appreciate. Otherwise at the beginning of each day we could interrupt the business appearing on the order paper by finding in some part of the country something which is undoubtedly urgent and of public importance to the people there; and in that way we would destroy the effectiveness of orderly debate. I therefore feel that we should interrupt the course of debate only if the matter is one which cannot be discussed otherwise.
Let me point out this fact. Although the Leader of the Opposition urged that there was urgency to discuss this matter, he had an opportunity on Monday to make a motion with respect to this matter, and again on

Inquiries of the Ministry Tuesday if his first amendment had been disposed of. The same statement applies to other members of the house. The supply motion is broad enough, even though the first amendment related to a dominion-provincial conference, for one to suggest that this matter might be the subject of a conference between the federal government and the province of British Columbia in order to see how this service might be restored.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FERRY SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: D.E.W. LINE    STATEMENT ON CLEARANCE FOR VISITORS
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition, as reported on page 859 of Hansard, asked the following question:
In view of the statement of the Prime Minister in the house a few days ago that Canada has now taken over responsibility for the administration of the D.E.W. line, is there any necessity now for a Canadian to secure clearance from any United States authority in order to visit that line?
May I say this, that I made the situation most clear on August 16 and August 18 last in regard to similar inquiries by the hon. gentleman. The answer was then and still is, no. I make that very clear and unequivocal with regard to the portion of the statement contained within the hon. gentleman's question to the effect that Canada has taken over responsibility for administration of the D.E.W. line, I should make it very clear that it is the operational control and not the administration of the D.E.W. line which was taken over by the R.C.A.F. The D.E.W. line is still maintained by the United States and, as I said a moment ago, the answer to the question is an unequivocal no.
While I am on my feet, may I say that since I spoke here on August 16 and 18 last the spirit of partnership which has characterized the combined efforts of Canada and the United States in constructing and operating the early warning system of which the D.E.W. line is an integral part has been satisfactory, and I am sure that in this respect the Leader of the Opposition, whose experience in office brought him into contact with these defence arrangements, will agree with what I have said.

answer, I should like to advise the hon. member that the R.C.M.P. are acting only to preserve order in the situation in Newfoundland. Mr. Speaker, while I do not expect an octavo from Waldo concerning his credo on radiation on orders of the day, I wish to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare a question. Has the minister's attention been drawn to a press statement of Professor M. E. Kettner, of the University of Manitoba, to the effect that the radiation effects of strontium 90 can cause leukemia, cancer of the bones and long-range harmful genetic effects, and that the

rate of fall-out appears to be going up steadily as snow and rain bring more of the element to earth? In view of the serious nature of this problem, can the minister inform the house if studies and investigations are being undertaken by his department?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monfeiih (Minister of Naiional Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STRONTIUM 90  EFFECTS OF RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I did not catch the hon. member's introductory remarks to the question. I shall have to look it up in Hansard, and perhaps I can address him personally in respect to those. I was, however, anticipating the possibility of such a question, and I would say that since 1955 when the department began measuring radioactive strontium in dried milk samples, a gradual but small increase has been noted in radioactive strontium levels.
The maximum permissible concentration of strontium 90 in milk for regular consumption has been estimated as 80 micromicrocuries per litre. The estimates of strontium 90 available to us based on monthly analyses of samples from more than a dozen stations across Canada are well below the maximum permissible concentration. The levels that have been measured in Winnipeg are not out of line with those which have been observed for other stations in the country. The department is, however, continuing to keep a close watch on this matter.

speechtext:
the si cond reading of Bill No. C-3 to amend the Interest Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I move the second reading of Bill No. C-3 at this time because I think it is of the utmost importance that this parliament take action to place a ceiling on the fantastic and exorbitant interest rates and carrying charges which are being levied in this country at the present time. I suggest that this bill covers a subject of major importance because of the tremendous growth in credit of various kinds in recent years.
I hold in my hand the Bank of Canada statistical summary for December, 1958 and it shows that in September, the latest month for which statistics are available-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Order. If the hon. member will allow me to interrupt, may I ask hon. members who are about to leave the house to make their departure expeditiously and those who are not about to leave it to moderate their tones so we can hear the hon. member.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Statistics for the last month available show, with respect to the various kinds of finance companies and credit extended by retail dealers to consumers, that the balance outstanding was the tremendous sum of $1,947 million. I am going to go on to indicate some of the fantastic interest rates that are being charged, and I suggest that if the bill before the house were passed it would result in the saving of tens of millions of dollars for Canadian consumers. It would place a ceiling on interest rates of 12 per cent per year, whereas in the sum of $1,947 million to which I have referred interest rates of double that amount or more are involved.
To demonstrate to the house how much saving there would be from the passing of such a bill one need only point out that if there were a reduction of 10 per cent in the credit extended, for example, it would mean an annual saving of some $195 million. With such statistics placed before the house I think one can understand the importance of this subject.
Credit is important to our country, consumer credit, instalment credit, credit obtained from small loan companies. These various types of credit are very important to commerce and to the individual who is able to obtain credit. Statistics I have here show that the total amount of such credit in 1951 was $706 million and that by September, 1958, this had increased to $1,947 million.


This tremendous sum of money is made up as follows: instalment finance companies, total credit of $752 million; small loan companies issuing instalment credit, $18 million; cash loans by small loan companies, $373 million; credit outstanding by departmental stores, $256 million. These figures total $1,399 million, and one must add to that the amount of credit provided by other retail dealers, making a grand total of $1,947 million.
One of the important kinds of credit is instalment credit. Various examples of the tremendous rates that have been charged have been placed before the house on previous occasions. The interest charges accompanying instalment credit range from the very low level of 10 or 12 per cent up to the very high level of some 54 per cent per year. There are companies that find the return in providing instalment credit and charging high rates of interest so lucrative that it is reported they are most anxious to promote the instalment end of their business even at the expense of cash sales.
In the whole field of instalment credit the great retail corporations are charging exorbitant rates. I have placed on the record on previous occasions the very high interest rate for instalment credit charged by Eaton's and Simpsons-Sears. The smallest purchase one can make from these companies under the instalment plan is an article worth $20 for which they make an interest charge of $2.25, with payments at the rate of $5 per month. This works out to an annual interest rate of 54 per cent. On previous occasions I placed this figure on the record, and at the time some members questioned whether or not the mathematics were accurate; but no one has yet shown that this figure is in any way inaccurate. I suggest to hon. members that such a rate should not be tolerated in Canada at this time. The purpose of the bill is to prevent such an exorbitant rate being charged.
A tremendous amount of instalment credit is involved in the purchase of automobiles, and the interest rates I have looked at range from 16 to 22 per cent per year. These rates are charged by the main companies in the field of providing credit for the purchase of automobiles. There are examples of companies charging much higher rates. I have in my hand a letter from the Middlesex Acceptance and Discount Company, London, Ontario, showing that on an unpaid balance a rate of 29.7 per cent had been charged. I suggest to hon. members that such a high rate is a disgrace to our country, and warrants action by members of parliament to see that such a high rate is prohibited in the case of automobile financing.

Another very large credit field in which huge interest rates are being charged has to do with second mortgages on houses. The government has provided excellent legislation for the purchase of homes. Even in the purchasing of homes, where large amounts of credit are available at lower rates of interest, it is often necessary for a purchaser to obtain a second mortgage, and in the buying of older homes the rates are often very high indeed.
In 1958 the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) placed some concrete examples on record showing the very high rates that are being charged on second mortgages. One example he gave at that time indicated that where a person wished to obtain a second mortgage for $4,250 he not only had to pay what I would suggest was a very high rate of interest, 7 per cent, but in order to get a mortgage of this size he had to pay a bonus of $750 and sign a mortgage for $5,000. Other examples were placed on the record by the hon. member for Vancouver East. He showed in the case of the example to which I have just referred that the interest rate worked out to 15i per cent. Other examples involved interest rates of varying amounts, but all of them were in that general range.
The passage of this bill would prevent such high interest rates being charged on second mortgages for home owners. This bill as it is now drafted would not apply where the interest rate is limited by a particular law. It would apply to interest rates that are not controlled by a particular law. Since that is the case, this bill would reduce to 12 per cent per annum the interest rate that may be charged by small loans companies making loans in excess of $1,500.
In 1956 we had a very long and very useful discussion both in the house and in the standing committee on banking and commerce with regard to the whole question of interest rates charged by small loans companies. Although the government at that time was reluctant, and although many members of the Liberal party in the banking and commerce committee at that time commenced by questioning the very purpose of the bill that was before the committee, I suggest that as a result of pressure of public opinion, sound arguments from those who approved of further controls on small loans companies, and some very definite pressure by the then minister of finance, Hon. Walter Harris, that bill was recommended by the committee to the house and subsequently passed. As a result of the passage of the bill there was an increase in the area of control from a ceiling of $500 on loans made by these companies to a ceiling of $1,500.
Interest Act
The effective rates that small loan companies are allowed is still high. Beyond the $1,500 there is no control, and there is no limit. I have in mind an advertisement, a so-called letter, which was sent to householders in Ottawa approximately a year ago over the signature of the manager of Pacific Finance Credit Limited, which reads as follows:
We will lend you up to $3,000 to consolidate your debts. Why not call me at Central 2-9476 and have a chat about it?
Yours truly
I believe the amount of $3,000 is suggested because if you obtained a loan of $3,000 there would be no control by parliament or anyone else on the amount of interest that could be charged. The passage of this bill would result in the control of interest rates charged by small loan companies on loans over $1,500.
Why are we asking that this bill be considered? We are asking the government to consider this bill because it is the ordinary Canadian who is paying these fantastic interest rates. Do I hear somebody say they do not have to pay them? If a young couple get married, they do not need a refrigerator or a washing machine or a home? They do not need this kind of credit? They can sleep on the street and they can eat at one of the neighbours? They do not need to buy all these articles to which I have referred? Of course that is not true. Canadians need credit. They have to have credit, and when they have to have credit they are forced to pay these fantastic rates of interest. I am suggesting that the government should take action in this field, and should study this whole question.
I have been in the house long enough to know that public bills introduced by private members are seldom passed. However, there are many instances in which the debate on a private member's bill has led to action by the government. I have no particular pride of authorship in the exact wording of this bill. I do submit that the principle contained in the bill is a good one, and it is something that the members of this house should study carefully.
I would ask the government to consider the possibility of referring this whole question to the standing committee on banking and commerce so we could go into this matter very carefully. I think it is time the government and parliament took action to remove Canadians from the clutches of loan sharks. These people are loan sharks, whether they masquerade as a respectable large retail firm or as a small loans company or as a company with a name like Beneficial Finance

Interest Act
Company. They are loan sharks and parasites, because they are charging these fantastic rates of interest which poor people must pay.
As we face a condition of recession and unemployment, then more and more people with smaller incomes will be forced to go to these companies to borrow money at these huge interest rates. One cannot argue that people pay these rates voluntarily, that they do not have to have the money. If there is sickness in the family, if an operation for a loved one in the family is necessary, if expensive drugs are necessary, the father of a family will pay any rate of interest, no matter how fantastic, to provide such essential medical service. I suggest those are the very items, these essential services, that place people in the hands of finance companies.
Perhaps another reason why people go to the finance companies is the type of high pressure advertising, the slick advertisements, asking people to come in and talk over their debts and their worries. I have in my hand an advertisement put out by Consolidated Finance Corporation, suite 26, Imperial Bank of Canada building, 171 Yonge street, Toronto. What does it say?
Here's the answer to your debt worries . . .
The present high cost of living makes it often very difficult to meet the demands of all your creditors.
The result: you get phone calls and letters of demand from your creditors, garnishees on your pay, court judgments and seizures, lawyers' actions . . . problems upon problems.
Now. with one visit to the office of Consolidated Finance you can shed your problems. Simply make a list of all debts you owe for: hospitals, automobile, furniture, jewellery, groceries, doctors, lawyers, loan companies, etc.-then see us.
With one regular payment to Consolidated Finance all your debts will be taken care of . . . all your financial worries ended.
What soothing syrup that is.
Security or guarantors are not required. 99 in 100 people are honest-
The company, therefore, say they are not going to have many bad debts.
So act now-make a list of all your debts-pick up the phone and make an appointment with Consolidated Finance Corporation, Empire 6-3322.
Finally, at the bottom there is this:
We have a "heart"-in the "heart" of Toronto.
If you ever walk into this office I would suggest you are not likely to get out of their clutches for many years to come. The evidence that was brought before the banking and commerce committee in 1956 by the superintendent of insurance indicated some of the fantastic rates that are charged by small loans companies. I remember clearly that he brought in evidence to the effect that a small loans company in Toronto had

charged rates of 75 per cent a year. In a country like ours surely, it is time parliament took action to outlaw such fantastic interest rates.
Somebody no doubt is going to stand up and say, "Some of these things are all right. We might like to move in this direction, but the draftmanship of this bill is inadequate and inferior". Mr. Speaker, may I say this. One can obtain the best legal advice available to a member of parliament in the drafting of these bills; nevertheless one is always faced with that argument. This particular bill has been drafted in the general language that has been used in the Small Loans Act, namely clause 2, paragraph (a) which defines the word "cost".
In the evidence given before the banking and commerce committee by Mr. Varcoe, the deputy minister of justice, it was pointed out by him that the Small Loans Act which controls all charges made by small loans companies within a certain area has never been challenged in the courts, and in his opinion was fully within the constitutional powers of the federal government. I suggest that there is no question whatsoever that this bill is drawn in such a way that if it were passed by this parliament, its terms would and could be enforced.
When the deputy minister of justice was before the banking and commerce committee he was asked a number of questions. As reported at page 684 of the minutes and proceedings of the committee he was asked this question by Mr. Enfield:
Q. So the conclusion of the argument, then, is that any charges whatsoever under a conditional sales agreement by way of prior discount could, if we wished be regulated by an act?
A. That is correct.
Then again as reported at page 692, a question by Mr. Follwell:
Q. Mr. Enfield and I were looking at section 2 and we saw there that with respect to automobiles or real estate that the interest could be on whatever the agreed basis is.
A. Yes.
Q. That is a fact?
A. Yes.
And further down the page we find a question by Mr. Crestohl:
Q. Take these acceptance corporations.
A. As far as the acceptance corporations are concerned, they do not do what they are doing by virtue of any provincial law, but they do it by virtue of the fact that there is no federal law.
In other words these companies are able to charge these exorbitant rates of interest because there is no federal law to control them. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is a bill that warrants the support of the members of this house. I ask the members on the government side of the house to

allow this bill to come to a vote today, and to let hon. members express their own individual opinions as to whether or not they think action of this kind is necessary.
Under the former administration, the Liberal government, the situation used to be that a number of private members' bills and resolutions came to a vote. It is quite true that if there was one that was a particularly hot potato, perhaps it was talked out; nevertheless the former government over the years allowed a great many private members' bills and resolutions to come to a vote. But this government, with its overwhelming majority, seems to be timid and frightened with regard to the matter of allowing a private member's bill or a private member's resolution to come to a vote. The amount of courage, if I may use that word, Mr. Speaker, seems to be in inverse proportion to the size of the government's majority.
I suggest that the government should allow members of parliament to deal with these bills by way of a vote. Private members' days in the past, in my opinion, have been important. A private member's bill or a private member's resolution is allowed discussion in the house without the government being committed. When a vote on such a bill or a resolution is taken, an opportunity is given to members of parliament individually to say what they think of the bill. If that were done in this case I am confident that at least some members on the government side of the house would support the bill. If a bill like this were allowed to come to a vote when it is presented to parliament, I believe that as time goes on more and more members would come to support it and that we would come closer to the day when its provisions became law.
But if the government continues to take the attitude which it apparently takes, namely that no private member's bill and no private member's resolution shall come to a vote, that one government speaker after another shall be placed on the list, then the government is making a farce of the whole procedure for dealing with private members' motions and private members' bills. It makes a mockery of our procedures in this house. I would suggest that the government, from its own standpoint, is taking the wrong attitude. I think the government would be in a better position to bring forward worth-while legislation if it allowed members of parliament, by a free vote, to express their individual opinions on a given piece of legislation.
I appeal to the members on the government side of the house to allow this bill to come to a vote today. I know it is going to be argued that if you put a limit of 12

per cent on interest rates, you are going to make it impossible for people to obtain this kind of credit. I do not believe that for a moment.

on which the chartered banks operate goes down, the banks become less and less interested in a large number of small accounts and more and more interested in providing large loans to corporations. What do the banks do? Banks are very happy to lend money to these finance companies, these legalized sharks about which members of the present government are apparently prepared to do nothing. The banks are happy to carry these big loan accounts for the small loan companies, but they say "no" to the ordinary person who comes in for a small loan and who is often in dire need of money.
I suggest it is time that the federal government itself should enter the field of providing loans to ordinary borrowers at reasonable rates of interest. We have an industrial development bank in this country which is federally operated. Hon. members can, if they like, say this is socialism, and therefore bad. Everyone in parliament is in favour of it nonetheless; everybody votes for it. I suggest that if the chartered banks fail to do this job, as they are now failing to do it, it is time the government took action by providing a publicly owned banking system to furnish these loans. This could be done by a change in the system of operation of the industrial development bank or by some other means. It would provide some real competition for the chartered banks who are not doing a job in this field.
Another method which might be followed- and I think it would be a good method- would be to study whether or not credit unions in Canada could be given the full rights which are now provided to the banks. I believe that if the vast number of credit unions in this country were incorporated as chartered banks and if the government were to give them the same consideration as is given to the chartered banks the credit unions could expand even more rapidly in the future than in the past. On this point I might say that credit unions and people interested in credit unions all across this country are turning increasingly to the belief that the time will soon come when credit unions should be given a federal charter to make them in fact the peoples' banks of our country. If credit unions had this further power I think they would be able to expand their business and provide the type of credit which is necessary to meet the needs of the ordinary borrower in Canada.
I have no hesitation about moving this bill again. I think it is a blot on democracy and a blot on the so-called free enterprise economic system that ordinary borrowers should have to pay this fantastic rate of interest. We have in the C.C.F. group moved

similar bills in the past. We have never obtained full satisfaction, but in 1956 we made some substantial progress. I ask that this whole question be referred to the banking and commerce committee for a thorough study. In 1956 when the measure under consideration at that time was before the banking and commerce committee we had what were then dubbed by one hon. member, 50 men in grey suits, representatives of the small loans companies, sitting in as observers of the committee, some of whom gave evidence in an attempt to kill the measure which had been passed by the House of Commons on second reading and referred to the committee. We do not need evidence from this kind of people. We have heard their evidence. I think it is time we had brought before the banking and commerce committee representatives of farm organizations, representatives of labour organizations, representatives of credit unions and representatives of consumer organizations to see whether working together we can provide in this country a system of credit at reasonable rates of interest. I say that the 12 per cent ceiling prescribed in this bill is a very high one. It is one above which no interest rate in this country should ever be allowed to rise.

Mr. Speaker, in rising this afternoon to speak on this motion I feel my first action should be to offer some words of congratulation to the hon. member who has brought this motion before the house. I am sure the hon. member who introduced this motion did so from a motive of anxiety to serve the public in this regard. I know he feels, as many of us do, that on occasions there have been cases where some members of our society have paid what must seem to all of us, on the surface at least, exorbitant rates of interest. Certainly I have no quarrel with this bill, the aim of which is to bring relief to some of those people who find themselves from time to time in the position of having to pay two or three times the rate of interest at which most business people can borrow money.
I am sure, also, that the hon. member who introduced this bill did not intend to make it more difficult for the people of this great nation to borrow money. I think he intended to keep to a reasonable minimum the amount of interest a Canadian citizen must pay for the money which he has borrowed. I do not wish to labour the point, but I feel that this bill is important to my constituents and, therefore, that it is very important to me. It is, of course, all the more important to make sure that what I have to say on this

bill will not be misconstrued by anyone in this house. I will go further and ask the indulgence of the house in this regard for what I have to say, no matter how elementary it may be on this issue. The truth is that I am anxious to see no person, man or woman, wealthy or poor, pay more than a reasonable amount of interest for any sum of money which circumstances may require them to borrow.
I must confess, however, that I am greatly troubled about achieving the objective which this bill seeks to ensure. Both the hon. member who introduced this bill and myself wish to make sure that no one can be victimized by the imposition of extra rates and by having to pay interest rates which are higher than those at which money can normally be borrowed from institutions such as banks. Just as much as I am concerned with the possibility of hardships on my friends in having to pay excessive interest charges, I am concerned with the thought that my friends must be able to borrow money as well.
Here is where I find I have some difficulty with the bill proposed by my hon. friend who wishes to limit the interest rates payable by any person in Canada no matter how such a person may happen to borrow money and no matter in what circumstances he may have to pay it back. There are some things I should like to point out to my fellow members of this house all of whom are interested in protecting their constituents from usury. I am a business man. It is true that I am a small business man and as such I have very little knowledge of the workings of high finance and the involved financial transactions that occasionally are necessary to float a major industrial activity. My business is a small one and my dealings are therefore almost entirely with ordinary people who are accustomed to dealing with me in very small amounts of money.
I hope I may be pardoned, Mr. Speaker, for feeling, to some extent, capable of speaking on this subject from the point of view of the small businessman. I happen to represent these as a class. I shall perhaps be forgiven for attempting to portray the point of view of the ordinary working man who happens to be my best customer, my usual and political contact and who in fact is representative of the fine Canadian people who are my friends and constituents.
I must confess that my first concern about this bill, which I am sure is that of all those in this house or outside of it who are small businessmen like me, is the question of the effect such legislation might have on the possibility of the ordinary citizen being able to borrow money. I realize that more
Interest Act
than the borrowing potential of the ordinary working man is at stake. Certainly for some small businessmen and especially those engaged in new, small and as yet unestablished businesses, it is every bit as important as it is to the average working man.
Credit in today's scheme of living is extremely important. I could go further and say that credit is the most important factor in the economic life of working people today, second perhaps to the holding of a job itself. The extending of credit or financing of money is really one and the same thing to us. It makes no difference whether I extend credit to a customer or whether he borrows money to pay me, the purport of this bill could be instrumental in deciding whether or not I can do business with a customer. Certainly I do not want to do business with him if he does not have the cash in some cases, and in other cases he cannot do business with me if I cannot arrange on my own the credit to cover the particular business transaction we have in mind.
I believe that my last comment has really brought us into the heart of the problem, one that consideration of any legislation dealing with interest always brings to mind. We must provide or maintain an incentive for the people with money to lend money to those who need it. Expressed another way, people who have money do not want to lend it unless there is a reward for allowing someone else to use it. People can invest money in many kinds of business, the object of course, always being the same, to earn a profit. If there is going to be money available for loans the lender must be assured of a profit and he seeks the highest profit he can obtain.
A major factor in determining the amount of profit that is made in the money lending business is, of course, the interest rate. The interest rate is determined to a certain extent like the price of other commodities is determined and there is the consideration that you want to get the best price and still get a lot of customers. The borrower would like to get his money for nothing and somewhere in between the money-for-nothing viewpoint and a desire for large profit is a mutually agreeable rate of interest that must be reached before money will be loaned or borrowed.
The bill before us today does not attempt to set an interest rate for everyone but it does set a maximum interest rate which can be demanded or paid. If we are to make an intelligent decision on the merits of the proposed bill we are forced to consider the factors which influence interest rates. As in the case of other commodities which are bought and sold, there are such factors as market fluctuations in the money market.

Interest Act
Usually an overabundance of goods in a store leads to sales at cut prices. In the financial world large supplies of money available to borrowers usually means that the interest rate will have a tendency to go down.
We should also bear in mind that in those cases the lender is himself a borrower so we must consider not just the amount of money that a finance company, for instance, happens to have on hand during a particular year, but we have to consider the amount of money his financial supplier happens to have on hand. Sometimes the amount of money available in the consumer finance field is not quite adequate to meet the demand of the credit buying of the nation during a particular period and this relative scarcity in the secondary sources of supply puts an inflationary pressure on the interest rate right down the line. I do not pretend to be an economist but I do have some experience and know what the effect is on my friends and constituents when they find themselves unable to get the amount of credit they require from time to time.
The scarcity of secondary supply of money may mean not only that the interest rate may rise somewhat but the secondary result of the inability of the usual consumer credit supplier to meet the demand might mean that new sources of money supply may enter this field; that is, there comes a strain on friends, relatives, the pawnshop or perhaps the poor corner grocer who, at a time when he finds his usual credit supply being restricted, is not able to collect at the usual rate from his customers.
Somewhat analogous to the question of supply of money generally, is the question of the number of suppliers. It is a well-known marketing principle and in fact it is one of our strongest beliefs that healthy competition is a very important factor in keeping prices down. Therefore competition in the money lending field is an important factor in keeping interest rates down. There is at all times a natural limit on the amount of interest a person will pay to any of the usual established money lending or finance institutions. There is keen competition between the various companies or agencies engaged in the finance industry themselves. They all want the business and there is a natural pressure driving interest rates down from the usual marketing device of attempting to attract more business than the competitor by making the price of the goods cheaper. Applying that to money it simply means that people who wish to borrow shop for money in the same way they shop for anything else. They try to get the cheapest rate of interest.
As well as the competition within the industry itself there is competition from what

I will term irregular or casual sources of money supplied, that is, the friends or relative or occasional lenders. Such irregular sources of supply play a more important part as the scarcity of money becomes evident, or the cost of it from regular sources seems to be out of proportion to the amount of good the borrower feels the loan will do him.
So far I have only mentioned competition among the lenders as a factor in depressing the interest rates, but along with this of course is the other side of the picture, namely the demand for money, or perhaps the competition for money among the borrowers. Canadian people seem to have spending patterns which may vary almost like the weather. At certain times there may be a great rush of consumer buying on credit; at other times there may not be such a demand for that type of money but there is a great demand for finances for expansion of or investment in small businesses, for the development of a new idea or the possibility of industrial development.
The point I am illustrating is that not only may there be a great demand from one type of borrower, or a great amount of competition for one type of lending money, but there may be a demand for other types of lending money, and the competition therefore between the lenders as borrowers from their sources of supply may have an inflationary effect on the interest rate they have to pay which, of course, is felt all the way down the line.
I think I have perhaps said enough about the factors of demand and competition as inflationary or deflationary pressures and as factors affecting the interest rate; they are after all usually broad underlying factors, which the general public is hardly aware of. The most important factor in so far as most people are concerned is that simple word "risk". Certainly, if interest is the reward for allowing someone else to use your money, some part of the interest at least must be the lender's reward for taking the risk that he may lose his money. On an individual transaction the amount of reward by way of interest will set the limit on the amount of risk the lender will take. In plain English, that is the little gimmick that says whether or not the bank or the finance company, or my friends, will lend me money at all.
For the sake of convenience, I would refer to this as the immediate risk factor. It is immediate in the sense that it is the biggest single factor in determining whether or not I can borrow money at a particular time. I think I should now state that the one word that bothers me the most about this bill is that the rate of interest we would arbitrarily

set as a ceiling could fall short of the incentive required to cause any lender to lend money to my constituents or to anyone else at a time and for a purpose which might be a very good and sound reason for them to borrow at that time. In other words, maybe they could not get money when they needed it. I am distressed at the thought of any of my friends paying interest rates higher than those mentioned in this bill, but I am even more distressed at the thought that I might prevent them, or bar them completely, from getting money which might be desperately needed. I will not labour the point too much. I am sure we all have some acquaintance with situations where a very high interest rate is much less important than being able to get some money somehow.
This, of course, is the risk factor on the basis of the single transaction and the direct effect on the interest rate for that single transaction. Risk, however, has an over-all effect on the interest rate covering any particular class of borrowing. There are always some losses. These losses in the money-lending business are part of the cost of running that business. They are just as much an expense as the office help or the office rent. As part of the expenses of the business they must be covered by the selling price of the product. Every borrower, therefore, must pay part of the cost of the losses in his class since it is reflected in the price. That means that the interest will go up or down, depending on how losses have been lately on that class of loan.
Risk is so important-a direct factor and an over-all factor-that lending institutions are classed by the type of risk they run. To put it in another way, while one may lend money on business firms the other may lend money on mortgages and still others may finance only car purchases. It is easy, I think, to see why I am troubled by an arbitrary interest ceiling, when risk is such an important factor in setting the interest rate.
Perhaps it might help to deal just a little with some of the risk factors, such as the length of time of the loan. Obviously, the longer the loan the more chance there is that the borrower may become ill or lose his job, or have sickness in the family. Long term loans actually might see almost a complete change in most of the risk factors. Since it is so hard to judge what might happen, one good way of meeting changed conditions is to try to get as much security as possible for the loan. Security is, of course, merely a means of reducing the risk and the more security the easier it is to borrow at a lower interest rate.
Interest Act
I think I would be wasting the time of this house, Mr. Speaker, if I got into a long involved discussion of long term, highly secured loans. The bill before us would really affect only the short term borrowers- with little or no security. In this class I suppose the car financing and the personal loans are the two largest groups of regular finance dealers. There would, of course, be a host of unorganized lenders who might also be affected.
When I mention car financing, I think we should really consider other laws which enter into the picture and affect rates of interest. In Alberta, as in many provinces, we have a conditional sales act. The most important clause in that act about this subject is the clause limiting the action that may be taken to collect. The act simply says that if a car is repossessed by the finance company it can no longer look to the borrower or buyer for further payment. If the car is worn out when retaken, the sale price may not meet the balance owing and someone takes a beating. This is just another risk factor. Frankly, I feel that a direct effect of the bill before us will be to increase the down payment required on not just cars, but on trucks, tractors, household furniture, and so on.
I do not want to get involved in that very involved argument as to whether or not people should or should not finance so much. I want to leave it to them. I feel that my constituents are grown-up, sensible people, and are able to manage their own affairs. If they want to pay more cash down on a car they can. If they are not able to, our action here might prevent them from buying material things they want. I do not think I am stretching things when I suggest that they might have to keep on driving an old car or living in an old home, or not replacing old furniture because of the action we take here. We would then have defeated our own ends and possibly I would have a constituent mad at me because of the action I had taken.
I want to protect my people as much as I can. I want to help them in whatever way I can. However, I am a little afraid that the bill might not provide as much protection as we want and it might hinder in the manner I have suggested. I think we must give much thought to our most important safeguard, the good common sense of the ordinary Canadian citizen. His idea of what he wants or needs might not be the same as mine. Each of us may find himself thinking that our neighbours are unwise on some occasions in the way they handle their money. I have some friends who I think spend too much on sports equipment. Maybe they do not

Interest Act
make a big enough down payment. On the other hand, that is the nice thing about a free country. We can even be foolish if we want to. I think we must make haste very slowly in this matter. We do not want to make protection an unnecessary restriction on freedom. Here is a thought that must give us pause.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). For many years, the hon. member has been proposing a similar bill in the house, and I understand that when he uses the word "interest" in the bill, he means commission, brokerage, inquiry and other costs, since in all those financial transactions of chattels or movables, the finance companies do all they can to pass collection charges on to the borrowers. In a few moments, I shall give you a few examples of what I mean.
This bill would set a maximum interest rate on transactions between consumers and their creditors, in connection with deferred payments.
According to section 91 of the British North America Act, the legislation governing rates of interest is a responsibility of the federal government.
However, it must not be forgotten that property and civil rights come within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and that they alone may legislate in this matter.
However, since the interest rate in no way affects individual property rights, I believe it would be of service to the consumers if an interest rate were fixed for business transactions involving instalment sales.
In the province of Quebec, there is a chapter in our statutes which governs instalment sales. It has been in force since 1917. The act provides that the seller must require of the buyer, as first instalment, a certain amount in cash, the interest rate being fixed at f of 1 per cent. However, that law applies only to retail sales, not exceeding, in any one case, $800.
There are, however, several exceptions; the law does not apply to the purchase of ships, farm implements, stationary engines and cars, to name but a few items.
Unfortunately for Quebec consumers, this legislation on deferred payments is not fully enforced, and large department stores still

urge customers to buy on the instalment plan, by means of signs bearing the words "no down payment" in big block letters.
As the provincial act provides no penalty for delinquent dealers, it has practically no effect.
In the case of sales in the medium price range, as we know there are carrying charges, covering bookkeeping and administration, as a means of evading the law. Those medium price sales, apply to such items as washing: machines, refrigerators, radios, television sets and certain items of furniture. Charges levied by the stores on such items appear rather unreasonable. However, since the amount of the purchase is not too high, the purchaser eventually manages to pay off his debt.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, there is one field in which interest rates are excessive, burdensome, and usurious, and I refer to the sale of cars, where the item being financed has greater value and is priced higher.
According to statistics, about 70 per cent of car sales are financed sales and, as of 31 December 1957, companies had financed such sales to an amount of $639 million. In my law practice, I am constantly dealing with these rapacious and usurious firms, and I think it is in the interest of the people of Canada that they be told of the methods of operation of those companies. First of all, those finance companies are in competition, and in the past two years, they have been pressing car dealers to get their business. To get this business, they agree to give the car dealers a 25 per cent commission on new cars and 15 per cent on used cars for any amount financed under the sales contract. However, the commission is payable only when the purchaser makes his last payment. Besides appealing to car dealers, they buy space in magazines and newspapers, and time on the radio. You would think, on reading those ads, that they are out to do a favour to people willing to do business with them. They make a show of fair competition and draw customers by alluring advertisement. Yet, in some cases their interest charges run as high as 25 percent, on the grounds of the high cost of inquiries, investigations and commissions.
I would even say that sometimes their interest charges run as high as 35 per cent, in cases of refinancing. Let me give you an example. Suppose a buyer has had his car financed for 18 months and was charged, say, $200 in

carrying charges. Now suppose the buyer runs into financial difficulties and wants his payments spread over a 24 or 30 month period instead of 18 months. In that case, he has to agree to additional finance charges for the new period, based on the unpaid balance, which already includes the original finance charges. In this case the buyer has to pay interest on the original amount of interest that had been charged to him. Other companies are even bolder. At the time the buyer is signing his contract, he is asked at the same time, in the car dealer's office, to sign a note for the same amount as the contract, and the car dealer assigns both instruments, the note and the contract, to the finance company. If the buyer returns the car, he is not credited with the value at the time of delivery and required to pay only the balance, but the car is sold, and the finance company, as true owner, sues the purchaser for the note, under the Bills of Exchange Act, and the purchaser has no choice but to pay.
All those examples, Mr. Speaker, show that the government must take steps to protect people who have to buy on terms. Those finance companies are subject to no control at all, and do just about all they please. I believe the government should investigate their methods and put a stop to their cunning and their greed.
The hon. member for Assiniboia said earlier that, because of the methods they stoop to, finance companies are crippling this country's economy. In fact, many buyers are in financial trouble because finance companies are forcing them to pay money they do not owe. I realize that there are times when people have to borrow, because of particular circumstances, but then the government should protect them against callous, soulless profiteers.
A few years ago, Mr. Speaker, finance companies used to follow a certain policy, but today competition, high pressure and publicity are such that those companies do not know where to stop. I suggest that the government take steps to check their insatiable appetite.
Since 1956, we have had in our statutes legislation which governs small loans not exceeding $1,500. When that act was passed, finance company representatives complained before the committee on banking and commerce, of the predicament in which they were being placed, said that they would not
Interest Act
be able to stay in business. Since then, they have kept operating for the benefit of borrowers, and none of them ever went bankrupt or had to quit.
If after due inquiry, the government of the time adopted the right legislation for the welfare of the people of Canada and of the borrower, I wonder why the present government could not do the same regarding the interest rate charged by those big companies that are putting the squeeze on borrowers.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that a committee could be set up-we already have the committee on banking and commerce-and I agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) who suggested that this bill be referred to the committee on banking and commerce where these companies could be asked what profits they are making, and where borrowers' unions and other people concerned, like car dealers could be heard. I am sure that in his report that committee would suggest that a bill be introduced in the house like the one which was adopted when the Small Loans Act was enacted in 1956, an act that would protect the people of Canada.

I associate myself with all organizations which have protested against the attitude of chartered banks, and I again urge the caisses populaires to stand firm and to continue their good work. They can be assured of the full co-operation of the present member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I cannot speak for my colleagues, but I know others in this house share my views and feel that chartered banks are not acting in good faith, nor in the interest of the average Canadian, in seeking to cause hardship to the caisses populaires. The people are on the side of the caisses populaires because they are closer to the people than any other financial institutions.
I support the bill proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and I hope it will be passed.
