Mr. Speaker, I have no quarrel at all with the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, but I should like to enlarge somewhat the scope of the discussion on this bill, and in order to put before the house what I have in mind I think it would be a good thing for me to read section 2 of the act as it now exists and, also, the proposed amendment.
In chapter 156 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, section 2 of the act reads as follows:
Except as otherwise provided by this or any other act of the parliament of Canada, any person may stipulate for, allow and exact, on any contract or agreement whatsoever-
I should like to underline, at this point, the words "contract or agreement". The section continues:
-any rate of interest or discount that is agreed upon.
Section 2 as it is intended to be amended, reads as follows:
Except as otherwise provided by this or by any other act of Parliament no person may stipulate, allow or exact on any contract or agreement whatsoever, a rate of interest in excess of twelve per cent per annum, whether it is called interest or is claimed as a discount, deduction from advance, commission, brokerage, chattel mortgage fees, or recording fees, or is claimed as fines, penalties or charges for inquiries, defaults or renewals or otherwise-
I should like to call attention to the presence in this section, also, of the words "contract or agreement".
If we refer to the act as it now stands we see, in section 3-hon. members will perhaps excuse me if it is more convenient at this point to continue in French.

(Translation):
Section 3 reads as follows:
3. Except as to liabilities existing immediately before the 7th day of July, 1900, whenever any interest is payable by the agreement of parties or by law, and no rate is fixed by such agreement or by law, the rate of interest shall be five per cent per annum.
And I point out again that section 3 contains the word "agreement".
I am therefore led to think, Mr. Speaker, that one might question the applicability of the amendment now under debate and the authority of the parliament of Canada on this subject. The hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Meunier), in referring to that point, said that according to section 91, subsection 19, of the British North America Act, the federal government could legislate on money interest. And he went on to quote section 92, subsection 13 which says:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to property and civil rights in the province.
All hon. members will agree that the central government has the authority to legislate on interest, while the provinces alone have the authority to legislate in relation with property and civil rights.
At this stage of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I must recall an earlier statement of mine, when I said that section 2 of the Interest Act insists on the word contract or the word agreement and leaves open the rate of interest, but that section 3 of the same act stipulates that, in the absence of an agreement, the rate of interest shall be 5 per cent per annum.
Consequently, in the case of contracts between individuals, a doubt comes to my mind and I wonder if the central government has authority to legislate in such case.
As you no doubt know, Mr. Speaker, there are various constitutional theories. First, there is that of the unoccupied field. On that count, I must say some provinces, namely the province of Quebec, have already occupied that field, as my hon. friend for Papineau (Mr. Meunier), pointed out a moment ago. When he spoke of instalment sales in the province of Quebec, he said, in fact, that they came under the civil code, which also provides for a yearly interest rate of 9 per cent for a period up to 24 months.
There is also another chapter, in our civil code, concerning interest on loans. But other provinces have also legislated in the field of instalment sales, although I do not think they
Interest Act
did so in regard to interest rates particularly, but rather in regard to instalment or credit sales.
Chapter 34 of the Revised Statutes of New Brunswick, 1952, entitled "Conditional Sales Act" includes several provisions which are identical to those of the Quebec civil code.
The province of Alberta has also legislated in the field of instalment sales, and I would refer the hon. members to chapter 66 of the Revised Statutes of Alberta, 1955, entitled "An Act Respecting Agreements Relating to Sales on Time and to Cash Loans".
Mr. Speaker, a study of the provincial statutes shows that at least three provinces have legislated in the field of instalment sales, of long term or short term loans, or interest loans. Furthermore, there is another theory, that of ancillary powers. I still have some doubt in my mind about this, which I should like to outline to the house.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in 1919, I think it was, the federal parliament legislated in the field of bankruptcy. There was some doubt at the time, because bankruptcy impinged on civil and property rights, as well as on the jurisdiction of the provinces. The case was referred to the Privy Council, which stated that the federal government could legislate in the matter, because it was a case of ancillary powers.
I have no doubt, as I said, that the central government can legislate on interest rates, but can such legislation go as far as to require the parties involved not to go beyond a maximum rate of interest? That is where a doubt arises in my mind, and in view of this doubt and of the other reasons given in this house, particularly by my hon. friend from Papineau-in fact, this suggestion was made by the mover of the bill we are now considering-I feel that all aspects of this legislation should be referred to the committee on banking and commerce for consideration.
Neither 1 nor the members of this house have any doubt that finance companies, such as small loan firms, automobile financing firms or firms that loan money under provincial legislation on instalment sales, whether in Quebec or in other provinces such as New Brunswick and Alberta, are charging rather high interest rates. In many cases, they also charge heavy handling fees and investigation fees against which the people

Interest Act
must be protected. On the other hand, I feel there is some doubt as to the federal parliament's constitutional jurisdiction, and that great care should be taken to avoid infringing upon the provincial field of civil rights and property. For this reason and for those advanced by the hon. member for Papineau and other members, I therefore move the following resolution:
(Text):
For all the reasons I have given, because I have some doubt regarding the competence of the federal parliament to act in this regard because it seems to me it might be overlapping provincial rights, and for the other reasons given by the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Meunier), I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger):
That the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak at this time in connection with this bill, and an amendment of which I had no previous knowledge. However, it is my feeling that the amendment that was just introduced is a proper one.
At the outset of my remarks I feel I should state that it is my conviction that there must be some limit imposed upon the amount of money that people may borrow and upon the interest rates which they may be obliged to pay. The bill as presented here, however, in my view is too definite in that it states an interest rate of 12 per cent. That is the principal fault of the bill. I do not believe an interest rate should be set at 12 per cent or any other figure without there being held a full inquiry so that members of the committee could examine expert witnesses from the finance field, the lending institutions and banking institutions. There should be some opportunity for investigation and discussion of this matter other than the limited opportunity provided here today. We should not arbitrarily take out of thin air the figure of 12 per cent. Nevertheless I feel the bill is a good one and in that I seem to be in agreement with most hon. members who have already spoken this afternoon. I should now like to draw a distinction between this bill as it relates to financing and the small loans bill. I do not wish to enter into a discussion of the relative merits of the two bills but merely to discuss the different types of lending which are involved.
The present bill concerning interest rates, as I understand it, includes all forms of interest except that charged on small loans as

defined by the Small Loans Act. I feel that the subject of interest rates should be divided into three categories each of which has its peculiar problems. The first would be mortgage interest; that is, interest charged on mortgages held on land, or chattel mortgages which are properly secured. The second would relate to bank interest and the third to purchaser credit. Thus far today the main body of discussion has centered around the subject of purchaser credit which normally involves a lien or a conditional sales agreement.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) in opening the debate indicated the enormous volume of credit financing that is taking place in Canada. In one sense he may have refuted his own argument. The volume of credit buying in Canada indicates that we must not act in such a way as to completely discourage such buying or cause the drying up of credit purchasing. It may be that imposing a limitation on interest rates would not have that effect but I feel that the imposition of a maximum of 12 per cent would have a detrimental effect on credit buying in general.
I should like to talk about loan sharks for a moment. Rather free use of that term has been made in the house today and X am not sure all of the comments made in this connection are justified. I do not dispute the fact that we have loan sharks in Canada. No one would be so naive. But perhaps we are being unfair to some of the larger companies who carry on well established businesses that are closely scrutinized and whose operations are aboveboard, to refer to them as loan sharks.
I was interested to see what a shark was, and I sent out for a dictionary. It says that the shark has not this name for nothing; that he will make a morsel of anything that he can catch, master and devour. I think that is the definition that the hon. member for Assiniboia places on the word and I agree that there are such people. However, I understand that there are some 150 purchase credit companies in Canada. Perhaps among the smaller of these there are very bad practices followed; in fact, I know there are. The main companies are the Industrial Acceptance Corporation, General Motors Acceptance, Traders Finance and Canadian Acceptance Corporation. These four companies handle 80 per cent of the business of purchase credit companies in Canada; the other 146 companies handle comparatively smaller amounts of business. I do not think we should say that all of these companies are loan sharks. I am not rushing to defend them but neither do I think we should be unfair.

I should like to speak for a moment on the three types of interest which I previously mentioned. Firstly, there are the mortgage loans. I would be inclined to agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia that on mortgage loans perhaps a maximum of 12 per cent interest, on a properly secured land mortgage, would not be unreasonable. Certainly, the average rate over the last 20 years at least that I have been in the practice of law has run from, let us say, 4J per cent to 8 per cent, and examination of previous documents indicates that mortgage interest very seldom ever rose above 8 per cent per annum.
There is the present difficulty of discount mortgages, and the hon. member for Assiniboia mentioned the fact that the interest rate is actually carried at a certain amount but when the mortgage is discounted the interest rate goes up. I think that we should not try to legislate mortgage interest on a sale basis. After all, when a person puts a mortgage on the market he wants to sell it and get cash. A lot depends on the buyer and what kind of land security he is paying for, how long the term is, whether it is a first or a second mortgage, and whether the owner of the property is in good circumstances. But, on the question of original mortgage loans, I would think that 12 per cent might be a reasonable maximum.
I now turn to the second type, namely that of bank interest. There again perhaps 12 per cent might be a reasonable maximum. The banks are very careful with respect to the people to whom they lend and in fact are at times unduly restrictive. A good many people who would like very much to obtain small loans are in this position: Because they have not had a previous history of any kind with a bank they are unable to secure bank loans and that puts them into the hands of the third class of persons I mentioned, namely the purchase credit companies.
I feel that to set a maximum of 12 per cent for this group of people would be unreasonable. I think the rate would be too low because the people who cannot get a mortgage loan on their real estate, either a first or second mortgage, or the persons who cannot get a bank loan, are not in very good financial circumstances. I have no doubt that that is the type of person that the hon. member for Assiniboia intends to protect, a person who just has to have some money and he cannot find anyone who will give it to him on a normal basis. I feel that to put too low a maximum on the amount that a person can borrow, or at least the interest rate at which the person can borrow, would not bring about the desired result. I am afraid it would dry up the small loans and the purchaser credit.

I think we would in fact be saying to a man who is desperate for money, "We know you need the money; we are sympathetic with you; you have tried everyone. We want to protect you; we know you cannot get your money at 12 per cent but that is your tough luck and we are going to protect you whether you want it or not." I am afraid that that might be the result of setting that rate of interest.
Some of the securities and risks undertaken by purchaser credit companies are pretty serious ones, particularly on motor vehicles and appliances. They are most difficult to repossess; they are subject to being damaged to such an extent that they are useless in a very short time and in a good many cases it is very difficult for them to recover. Therefore, the risk being higher, the rate of interest must be higher.
I am not here to speak for the finance companies. On the contrary, I practise law in a town where I am constantly consulted by people who are in what the hon. member for Assiniboia would call "the clutches of the finance companies". Time after time I have had people come to see me who have felt that they have been badly used in their dealings with a company. I have had people tell me that they had entered into certain deals on misunderstandings and that they regretted them. Therefore, I see the problem from the point of view of the person who has to deal with a purchase credit company, particularly in connection with automobiles. I am not sure that it is always the fault of the company. I think that the dealers come in for their share, and in a good many instances the dealers who are anxious to make sales take the papers and turn them over to the finance company in such a way that the finance company lends the money but really takes a bad security. In a case such as that, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the dealers in many instances are actually agents, not in a legal sense but in an actual sense, of the finance companies because they accept the forms and they fill out the papers that the purchaser requires and then sell them to the finance company. In an instance such as that a good many members of the public are not given a good deal, but I am not sure that the interest rate has very much to do with it. I think probably out of five cases that I have had to deal with recently at least two of them were the result of a person being very stupid in entering into a transaction that he should never have gone into. I think it is the experience of the house that you cannot legislate against stupidity nor can you legislate to protect people against their own actions when they know full well what they are doing.

Interest Act
I should like to speak for a moment on another matter, the interest rate placed in the forms that are presented to the buying public. A lady came to me one time and said to me, "I have found just about the best finance company I ever heard of. They are lending money at 2 per cent. I just filled out a form today and they lent me $500 at 2 per cent. I never thought there was a finance company like that in Canada." I said I should like to see the form and she brought it to me. The figure "2" had been inserted in the contract but in the small print were the words "per month". She had signed a contract to pay 24 per cent per annum rather than 2 per cent.
If we are to give thought to what rate a person may pay we should also give thought to making it very clear to people what they are paying, and the use of an interest rate per month should not be allowed. This is very much in keeping with other sections of the Interest Act relating to regular monthly payments which specify that a mortgage must contain the exact interest rate per annum which is being charged. I think that is one instance where people are often misled. They think at the time that 2 per cent is not very much and they do not realize what is meant until they read the contract in full.
In 1957 sales of merchandise which was financed amounted to over $1 billion. These were goods sold and distributed to the public through instalment buying. If instalment buying were not encouraged these goods would not have gone to the public. They would not have been marketed. There were one million individual accounts opened by people and of this figure 70 per cent was handled by the known finance companies and the other 30 per cent by people who do their own financing. I merely point that out to indicate that for the sake of the economy of the country we should not take action that would reduce too much the legal maximum interest rate because it would have the effect of diminishing the purchasing power of the public and also of drying up credit for people who would like to buy.
Certainly it is my own feeling that credit buying for the individual is not a good thing. I feel, as do a good many other people I know, that if you cannot afford a thing you should not buy it. However, that seems to be just about the last theory that most people in this country follow.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I am in agreement with the principle of the bill but I am not in agreement with the arbitrary setting of the rate at 12 per cent. I think it is too low and that it would have an adverse effect. If we were to go into the matter in a

committee perhaps we might find out what the effect of the Small Loans Act has been. As the hon. member for Assiniboia said, it may not have been as serious as the companies have indicated. If we had such an examination I think we might be able to arrive at a rate of interest which, while maintaining the purchasing power of the people and keeping credit available, would still be sufficient to protect the general public from their own folly and from the absolute necessity of paying exorbitant rates. I have been speaking on the amendment and I am in favour of referring this whole matter to a committee.

I should like to say at the outset that I realize, and I dare say most members of the house do, that there are problems with regard to money lending in this country. We all know the hardships that young married couples have to face in order to establish themselves and provide security in the form of a home, furniture and so on for the family that they inevitably intend to raise. We know that in order to acquire a home they must take out a mortgage'and, normally, must pay interest. We know that a great many of them, in order to buy furniture, must finance it either through the small loans companies or through the firm from which they purchase the goods. Can these really be considered problems or are they something that is part of our way of life today?
I think the statistics enunciated by the hon. member who introduced this bill would indicate that credit today is a growing part of our society and is a business common to free enterprise countries. Those who have spoken on this bill thus far have presented their views for and against, but the majority of those who have spoken have spoken in favour of it. I should like, for a moment, to direct the attention of the house to some of the arguments that could be advanced for the other side.
First of all, I would say that a bill of this nature which is introduced to restrict interest rates to a certain percentage is a very important bill and should not be considered lightly by this house, should not be considered in a hurry. I feel therefore, that the amendment that has been presented is a good one, and that the bill should in fact be referred to the committee. There is, without a doubt, a need for money-lenders in this country. As I mentioned before, the statistics quoted by the hon. member for Assiniboia indicate this need. However, I should like to point out also that many of these statistics that were presented to this house today have been presented by him in past speeches, and to a large extent those statistics have not been revised, even to the
Interest Act
extent of two or three years ago. I feel that it is impossible to accept those statistics because they are obviously not up to date.
We have not, either in this debate or in past debates on this topic, received a satisfactory explanation as to how the figure of 12 per cent is arrived at. I feel we would be doing an injustice to our country and to our economy if we introduced legislation restricting interest rates for the simple reason that we felt they were too high. I am sure we could find people in the country who would say, no matter what figure we introduced, that the rate was either too high or too low. I feel that in order for this house to arrive at a decision that 12 per cent is in fact a fair figure we should have some indication as to how this figure was arrived at. I should like also to point out that the figure of 12 per cent, as applied to a department store, means this: if someone goes into a department store and wishes to purchase a $20 article which he finances for three months, under this legislation the most interest that could be charged would be 60 cents. I wonder whether or not that is a sufficient charge to enable the company to economically carry the necessary expenditures to provide a staff to accommodate the public who wish to open charge accounts.
I should like also to point out at this stage that in the past the hon. member for Assiniboia has introduced legislation dealing with small loans companies. I would say that if such legislation were passed, and if the bill now before us were passed he would be paving the way for unregistered money lenders to charge a higher rate of interest than registered money lenders would be able to charge. He would be working in reverse, so to speak, because instead of being able to charge a little more interest for a small loan a person would be held to a certain percentage for a small loan which would be less than the one per cent per month for which this bill provides.
I do not pretend to be an expert in finance nor an expert in credit, and I would say that I do not believe the hon. member for Assiniboia is holding himself out as an expert in finance. However, it is interesting to note that in the course of his remarks he has used such phrases as "fantastic and exorbitant interest rates". He used the term "loan sharks", and talked about saving the Canadian people tens of millions of dollars if this bill were passed. I suggest that these are his opinions and it is the duty of this house to find out if those statements are really based on fact or if they are merely propaganda to appeal to the voters of this country and to persecute institutions that are, in fact, trying to carry on legitimate operations and give

Interest Act
the public a service that they evidently need. I should like to indicate to the house what might possibly happen if legislation were passed which set interest rates too low.
First of all, I think it is quite obvious that if interest rates were too low and a profit could not be made a great many of the small loan companies would immediately liquidate and go out of business. I think that would lead us right into a black money market because I think everyone will agree that if there is a need for money, then the person who wants to borrow will always find someone who will lend it to him regardless of what legislation may be passed by the federal government. In this connection, I would point out that these statements of mine are borne out by publications dealing with the same situation in the United States. It has been found that in states where the interest rates were too low the loan companies immediately liquidated and left those states. Then the true loan sharks came into operation from neighbouring states and charged as much as 500 per cent interest. I think that is a thing we all want to avoid because by bringing in legislation which places interest rates too low we are bringing about the very thing we are trying to avoid.
Then, this question could be asked: If interest rates were set too low, from where would the people borrow who wished to borrow? Keference has been made to the second mortgage business. I suggest that in this business there is a great deal of risk in connection with certain second mortgages. I have had some experience with them. A young couple who wish to buy a home may find themselves in a position where they do not have a high enough down payment in order to get a home through the National Housing Act. They therefore purchase a private home. In order to do that, they need a second mortgage. I have seen people pay as little as $500 down on a house and then finance it with mortgages. That procedure certainly involves risk as far as the lender of the money is concerned because if real estate drops by a mere $500 he can be out of pocket that amount and indeed more, if account is taken of his expenses.
I should like to mention to the house-and I am sure everyone will agree-the fact that no one is compelled to borrow money. The hon. member for Assiniboia stated that the only people who borrow money, or the majority of people-I do not want to misrepresent him but I believe he said this-in his opinion, who borrow money from finance companies or from small loan companies are people who have heavy doctor bills or hospital bills to pay. I again submit to the house

that this is his opinion only. He has not given us any facts to back up this statement. Before any legislation of this kind is passed I think we should have the facts before us, and should find out just who are the customers of these small loan companies.
I may say that when I noticed this bill on the order paper I did a little bit of investigation on my own. If the hon. member would take the trouble to ask some of these people who are in the business, instead of criticizing them all the time, he would find out some of the facts. I submit to him that the small loans companies, financial companies and money-lenders all across Canada do business with people who come back to them when they want money again and who refer other people to them. I suggest to the hon. member that some of these farfetched examples of his are extreme cases and are the exceptions rather than the rule. I therefore think it is a good idea to send this bill to a committee so that these facts would come out in the open and we would find out just how authentic are some of the wild statements made by the horf. member for Assiniboia.
The hon. member for Assiniboia has classified anyone who lends money as a loan shark. I find that classification difficult to follow and difficult to go along with.

Mr. Speaker,
I have had dealings with these companies and I think they are doing a very good job in this country. They are reputable concerns. People have enough confidence in them to purchase annually goods worth millions of dollars. I certainly refute a statement of

that nature. I should like to say that there are in this country so many department stores that competition is extremely keen in the department store field. Hence if any one department store were making any finance charges that were out of line with those of another store, I think the people would soon realize what was going on and would go to the place where they could get the best bargain. I think the hon. member will agree that is only human nature.
The hon. member has stated that a great many people are brought in to these small loans companies because of their advertising program. I am not disputing that statement. I think possibly there is some merit in it. However, to single out one group in our society on that score is wrong. I think the hon. member will be obliged to agree that advertising today has on the whole degenerated to a level which is not to be considered right. I suggest to him that even the advertising of his own party has degenerated to that level.
By controlling interest rates are we not in fact controlling profits? For instance, if I have a certain amount of capital that I wish to lend and if the House of Commons sets the interest rate that I may charge on that capital, they are in fact controlling the profit that I may earn in what I choose to be my means of every day living. I suggest that a step of that nature is the thin edge of the wedge and that it is definitely a step toward socialism. Every piece of legislation that is passed by a government infringes, to a certain extent, upon a right of the individual in a free enterprise system. If we are to pass a bill to control interest rates and to control the profits that certain people can make, then should we not go further and control what other people can make? I suggest that that is socialism, pure and simple, and I for one would not like to see it come about.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was endeavouring to outline some of the arguments which could be advanced against this bill by persons or firms engaged in the money-lending business. I was also endeavouring to point out to the house that a great many of the statements made by the hon. member for Assiniboia were merely an expression of his personal opinions and did not appear to be founded on fact.
Interest Act
I realize, as do other hon. members, that there are persons engaged in the moneylending business who, it might be said, persecute some individuals who borrow from them; or, at least, that there are people engaged in this business who follow unscrupulous practices, but I do not think it is fair for us to include everyone engaged in the money-lending business in this category and label them as loan sharks. There are, it is true, loan sharks in our society; these are the ones we want to keep from getting a hold on any individual.
For these reasons I think this bill should be sent to the committee in order that both sides of the argument may be analysed and in order that the committee may be able to bring back to this house a report which could be accepted and which would be founded on fact.
I am one of those who always try to look at both sides of the question and refrain from making any prejudgment, and I do not feel it is within the province of any hon. member of this house to make wholesale accusations against those engaged in any type of business. I feel that these are also the views of this government and that when a committee, after having heard both sides of any argument, makes a report to this house, that report will be proceeded on in fairness to both sides. I believe the committee could work out a ceiling percentage which would be acceptable both to those who are engaged in the business and to those who rely on these firms and individuals for financial aid when required.

speechtext:
The amendment which has been moved means in effect that approval should not now be given to the principle of this bill but rather that the measure should be given further consideration in the banking and commerce committee.
As the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) stated, he welcomes the possibility of this bill, or a bill such as this, being referred to the banking and commerce committee for complete investigation and for possible amendment if the committee, after investigation, found amendment to be necessary. We are a little concerned that so many members of the house do not wish at this time to express endorsement of the principle of the bill and that they should wish to have it referred to the committee before endorsing the principle. I have no qualms of conscience at all about being ready to endorse the principle of the bill at this time. I do not see why we cannot endorse the principle that there should be a limit placed on the activities of those who are engaged in moneylending. The hon. member for Winnipeg

Interest Act
North (Mr. Smith) went to considerable length to bring out his opinion with regard to the comments made by the hon. member for Assiniboia. He accused the hon. member for Assiniboia of expressing opinions rather than making statements of fact, and attempted thereby, I believe, to minimize the effectiveness of the wonderful speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Assiniboia.
It may be recalled that about a year ago I placed on record a case in which a man had been charged an interest rate of 235 per cent. I had all the evidence on that case with me on that occasion. I have here another case-the case of Mr. and Mrs. Wag-enstein of the town of Port Coquitlam who have asked me to use these facts in the hope that some legislation might emerge or in the hope that at least other people will not be taken for a ride in the way they were. The Wagensteins are a very honest and reliable couple living on Hastings street, and on one occasion they needed some money. They have a home which I would value as being worth at least $15,000; even at a sheriff's forced sale it would bring in not less than $10,000. On January 19, 1955, they needed a loan and they gave their home as security. It was a first mortgage; there was nothing owing on this house at all, and the house was practically new. They obtained a loan of $2,400 in return for which they had to sign a mortgage for $3,000 repayable at $75 a month, with 7J per cent interest, not on the $2,400 but on $3,000. They received only $2,400. They had to repay the principal of $3,000 plus 7J per cent interest on $3,000.
The Canadian Bank of Commerce at Vancouver-the Shaughnessy branch at 3070 Granville Street-acted as collection agency for the lady who had supplied the money, a Mrs. Anderson of the city of Vancouver. Here is a case of a chartered bank receiving monthly payments on behalf of Mrs. Anderson, issuing a passbook and registering the monthly payments as they were made. By means of monthly payments this loan was completely repaid in three and a half years. I have been looking over the facts as indicated in this passbook and I find that not only did Mr. and Mrs. Wagenstein pay a bonus of $600 but they also paid interest totalling $398.59. In other words, for the use of $2,400 repayable monthly over a three and a half year period they had to pay a total in charges of $998.59. This, on $2,400 over that length of time, means a real interest rate of 23 per cent. Mr. Speaker, this money should have been available to Mr. and Mrs. Wagenstein at 5 per cent or, certainly, at not more than 6 per cent

interest. If that had been the case they would have saved themselves approximately $800.
The reason why I mention this particular case is because I have permission from the people involved to do so. Another reason is that we in this group hope that by putting actual instances on the record it will help the cause a little bit. Still another reason is that I want to emphasize the point that here is a skilled worker, a toolmaker who is employed in a mill. His services are much in demand and he has never suffered because of unemployment. Although he receives a fairly decent monthly income this man and his family have been robbed-I cannot think of a more apt word-of $800 of purchasing power which was lost to them. This type of thing is going on all across Canada. Canadian people are being robbed of purchasing power which they badly need at the present time to pin-chase the necessities of life and to supply employment to agricultural and other producers in this country. I certainly hope the amendment at least, if not the bill, will be allowed to reach a vote.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the family in the case the hon. member has cited is so well established with respect to employment and income, why did the gentleman concerned have to borrow money?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I did not ask him why he
needed $2,400 at that particular time but there are many reasons why people have to borrow money from time to time. I may say that this family had a little girl in the hospital for almost a year and a half not very long after this incident occurred. There can be cases of sudden illness and many other reasons why people must borrow money at various times.
The gentleman also told me that he went to the bank but the bank was not very interested in supplying him with money over a three and a half year period. It is common knowledge that banks in general are not much interested in lending money for periods of that duration. I have cited this case because the people in this community know the family to which I have referred and they know it is a bona fide case. They know that the family deserved to receive credit at a nominal rate of interest.
We always hear a great deal about the risk involved in lending. In the case of automobiles the finance company runs no risk whatsoever. It is the agent who sells the automobiles who

must underwrite each vehicle that is financed by the finance company. If the purchaser fails to meet his payments and the amount cannot be recovered from the sale of the automobile the agent must make up any loss the finance company may have sustained. They run little risk indeed as is shown by their financial returns.
To say that finance companies lend money with little or no security is, I feel, also not in line with what actually takes place. From my observations the security they obtain usually far exceeds the value of the loan they make. They do not run much of a risk. I fail to see the logic of limiting by law the operations of reputable institutions in this field. There is a maximum that chartered banks cannot exceed. Most credit unions, I know, have provincial limits to meet that have been established to determine the maximum rates that they must not exceed. I cannot understand why so many hon. members feel that these other money-lenders should be exempt from limitations as to interest rates.
I sincerely hope we will follow this evening the usual procedure that has obtained for many years in this house, that is that when a private member has introduced a bill a cabinet minister or parliamentary assistant has replied on behalf of the government and expressed its attitude toward the proposition being put to the house. That practice was followed by the previous government. Either a cabinet minister or a parliamentary assistant would explain to the house the attitude of the government with respect to the idea being put forward in the bill. That has not occurred today but it may happen yet. As the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out, we usually had a chance to have a vote on private bills. Even although a cabinet minister had spoken against a bill, very often six, twelve or as many as eighteen backbenchers of the government rose at the time of the vote and by so doing endorsed the principle of the bill then being proposed. I should certainly like to see that happen at this time. In that way hon. members who are supporters of the government can show that they also are concerned with the welfare of the ordinary people of Canada who, as has been admitted, must have credit from time to time.
I should like to add this further thought. It is not only the individual consumer who is being penalized by these exorbitant interest rates. There are many small businessmen in Canada who at the present time have to patronize money-lenders who charge extravagant interest rates. I have even spoken to hotel owners who have told me the only way they could obtain money for necessary 66968-9-62
Interest Act
renovations was to deal with finance companies and pay interest charges of an exorbitant nature. These high rates of interest are a burden on the economy and they also impose misery and hardship on that section of the population with which this parliament should be most concerned, the ordinary people of Canada who need its help. The finance companies do not need the help of this parliament and they are not asking for it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words in taking part in this interesting debate are to express envy that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) should have somebody come to his door and offer to stake him to a sum up to $3,000. This has never happened to me.
There has been an interesting dispute here for part of this afternoon and evening as to whether those who charge high interest rates may properly come under the classification of loan sharks. I am one who disagrees emphatically with this designation. I offered a description of these people last year and I proffer it again to the house for what it is worth. All of us are familiar with the phrase, "men in grey flannel suits". I paraphrased it by saying, "men in grey fleece suits". Furthermore, I think that the designation is probably improper. It does not properly describe the habit of fish. In this case, we are trying to say that the loan sharks throw the bait at the people.
In the last year there has been one significant development in the credit field of Canada, which has been alluded to only very briefly in the debate that has gone on so far today. I am thinking again of one of the largest banks in the country, namely the Bank of Nova Scotia, which has set up a subsidiary company which deals exclusively in the field of consumer credit. As the hon. member who preceded me has pointed out, the amount of interest that the chartered banks can charge is, I believe, six per cent. In any event for decades it has proved unprofitable for the chartered banks of Canada to get into the consumer finance field. I have talked to bank managers about this. It was their feeling that the loans were so small that it would take some time to check into the credit of the people asking for them. A great deal of bookkeeping was involved. There was always the risk of bad debts and the profit on a large number of loans could be wiped out if even only one person defaulted. Obviously, this is what has happened. The banks have not entered this field, not because they were unwilling to do so but because the rate of return was so low, or indeed nonexistent, that it would have been impractical for them to do so.

Interest Act
Since the Bank of Nova Scotia took the new step with this consumer finance company, I am informed that the new company is making a very sizeable number of loans at a rate of one per cent per month, which is 12 per cent per year, or the exact figure that the hon. member for Assiniboia has put in his bill which is before us today. I do believe that the effective rate of interest on this subsidiary company's loans, however, is just a bit over 10 per cent.
I do not want to get into the field of what should be charged for consumer finance and those other matters that were talked about this afternoon. I think we would get into a very tricky field indeed if we discussed that matter. It may be all right for somebody to suggest that 12 per cent, or some other arbitrary figure, is a magic number to cure all the ills, but I share the doubts which have been expressed by other hon. members that we can set any specific figure. I would go even further and say that we may have to consider a sliding scale of maximum interest charges. I would like to quote from a memorandum prepared by the Household Finance Corporation of Canada, which was presented for study by the council for social service of the Anglican synod of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. I should say that this is a treatise prepared by a finance company, but I believe it has excellent research facilities and that these words should be given some weight. Certainly, it was accepted by the church gathering that took place in my part of the world. I quote:
One important point which many people fail to recognize is that the costs of conducting a small loans business are dictated by the number of loans made rather than the total amount of the loans. An institution which could profitably make loans of, say $12,000 at six per cent per annum would find that it could not profitably make loans of, say $200 at the same rate. This follows because it would require 60 times the amount of time and effort to lend $12,000 in $200 loans as would be required to lend the same amount in one loan. Obviously the small loans must be at a much higher rate.
The banking and commerce committee of the 1938 House of Commons whose report formed the basis for the Small Loans Act, recognized this fact and expressed it in the following words:
"Quite obviously the purchase of a block of 12-year Canadian government bonds requires little expenditure for investigation and none for supervision; investments in 50 farm mortgages for varied periods entail considerable cost both for investigation and supervision; while the investigation of 1,000 applications to effect loans to 500 people for a few months with meticulous supervision becomes expensive business when expressed as a percentage rate of $100 on a monthly basis".
I continue from the submission by the corporation to the council for social services:
The above quotation emphasizes another important cost factor in connection with consumer loans- the cost of investigating the considerable number

of applications which do not result in loans being made. Currently household turns down 45 per cent of applications received.
By "currently" the company means January of 1958. I continue with the quotation:
This cost is considerable as the investigation of applications which do not result in loans is in many cases as extensive as for those which do.
The parliamentary committee referred to above expressed its main objective as follows:
"Throughout its inquiry your committee's objectives has been to secure the best procurable rate for the borrower".
It is evident from the exhaustive nature of the 1956 committee's examination that they had the same objective in view.
While keeping in mind that the rate should be set as low as possible in the interests of borrowers the original committee recognized that, for the same reason, it must also be high enough so that lenders would be able to continue to provide the service. This point is emphasized by the experience in certain of the United States.
That experience, Mr. Speaker, as was demonstrated by those who preceded me in the debate, was that when the wrong maximum interest rates were set; that is, set by whim without taking into account the market conditions, the supply of money and so forth, the companies folded up their tents and left the inhabitants of that particular state, or of those states at the mercy of money bootleggers, which would probably make the hon. member's conception of a loan shark pale compared to the reality of that type of person.
I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) who preceded me, on the problem of the Wagensteins who, to get a $2,400 loan, were forced to sign a $3,000 mortgage and pay the same back at $75 a month and in fact pay $398 interest and $600 bonus. I was curious to learn that a couple as reputable as they are should be placed in the position of not being able to obtain the proper credit facilities. It seems to me that if a couple has a $10,000 house, as my hon. friend stated they had, and the breadwinner of the family has a good job, it would have paid them very well to do a little bit of shopping around. There may have been a suggestion of criticism of the bank that my hon. friend mentioned in relation to the Wagensteins in refusing to lend them the money they needed at that time. I think it would be unjust criticism and should not go unchallenged on the record. I think there are many of us in the house who are familiar with the fact that a few years back it was difficult for the banks to make such loans. In any event, the banks have been traditionally chary about entering the mortgage field.

One should not be too hasty with any suggestion of acting improperly simply because they are the depositories of the amount of money that has to be paid by the mortgagors in this particular case. If my hon. friend had given further details to the house about the Wagenstein case I think we might be better able to make up our minds whether that case was in fact one of very great hardship or whether it was simply a case of a couple who, without proper advice or guidance, went into the money market and were consumed by the first shark who came drifting by.

speechtext:
My friend says that there are millions like these people, and perhaps there are. It seems to me though that the fact that people do have difficulty in handling money problems is not really a valid excuse for trying to protect them from harm. If they are not gypped by one type of person they will be gypped by another type of person and probably the better course is education rather than protection.
So that we can get some facts on the record I should like to deal with the type of person who borrows from the small loans companies. These facts were contained in a brief submitted to the banking and commerce committee of the House of Commons by the Canadian consumer loan association in 1956. I do not propose to put all the figures on the record. That was done last year by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) in a very thoughtful speech but I will recall some of the figures to the house. Taking loans as classified by occupation of borrowers, in the year 1954 craftsmen, foremen and kindred workers represented 30.21 per cent of those who borrowed from the small loans companies. Next in line were operatives and kindred workers, 21.60 per cent; then clerical and kindred workers, 10.57 per cent; labourers, but not farm labourers, 8.82 per cent; and so on down the line. A rather interesting point is that school teachers comprised only .64 per cent of those who went to small loans companies. Incidentally, the total number of loans made in that year was 707,530.
I think this house performs a useful function every time we discuss the Interest Act or the Small Loans Act. This has been proven today by the number of hon. members who have been able to cite specific examples of people in their own ridings who have been ill treated or have considered themselves ill treated and have taken their problems to their members, as they very properly should. It might be of interest if we turned from economic considerations and the statistics we 66968-9-62J
Interest Act
have been having today to something different. For the benefit of the house and the country I should like to give in brief form what is known as the constant ratio formula or algebraic device by which one can measure the extent of the interest rate one is being charged. If everybody is ready, Mr. Speaker, the formula is as follows: R equals 2CP divided by A (N plus 1). I will elaborate on this somewhat esoteric if bare algebraic formula. R is the annual interest rate; C is the interest or finance charge in actual dollars; P is the number of equal instalment payments in one year, exclusive of the down payment; A is the amount that is borrowed; and N is the number of equal instalment payments in the whole contract period exclusive of the down payment. I was trying to work out the interest that the Wagensteins paid to see if my hon. friend's arithmetic was correct but unfortunately he ended his speech before I could quite complete the mathematics.
Last year in dealing with this subject I noted that one of the big stocks in trade of the loan companies was their ability to prey upon the fears of people, to make the sweet pitch to them that by putting all their troubles in one basket they would, instead of having a dozen nagging letters about bills they could not pay only have to make one payment. Of course, this siren song does not reveal that if anything should go awry with that one payment they will get letters the like of which they had not received from the ordinary commercial businesses to which they had owed money. But this is a tempting point for a person in today's society, and I should like to emphasize again that the danger, of course, in consolidating these principal and interest payments and a variety of debts into one large debt is that you then find yourself in the position of paying interest on your interest, and so the snowball goes on rolling and the avalanche bears down on these people, some of whom are buried and become slaves to consumer finance companies for the rest of their days.
There is no substitute for common sense in knowing how to handle one's finances, there is no substitute for looking at the fine print of a contract and being canny about money matters. But I think the point has been well made by the members who have supported the bill that some protection must be afforded to people and I am thoroughly and heartily in favour of the bill. I am inclined to support the amendment although I hope it is not a device by which the bill will become buried. It might be better to throw out the amendment, approve the bill in principle and then get it before a committee thus approved in principle so that the

Interest Act
committee may hear, tor example, about the experience of organizations such as the Bank of Nova Scotia and how it has fared on entering the consumer finance field at a rate of 12 per cent compared with the companies that have been operating in that field at 15, 18 or 24 per cent over the last few years.
I say let us get their experience and the experience of other segments of society having dealings in the consumer finance field and then set a realistic figure. Again I would suggest that a proper method might be to adopt a sliding scale rather than an arbitrary ceiling.
For example, in studying the books and literature pertaining to consumer finance you will find that the smaller the loan the more costly the operation. Even if a person borrows only $100 his credit standing must be investigated in the same way as the person who borrows $500 or $1,000. Since I am informed that the cost of the investigation is about $20, it means that the person who borrows $100 does have that extra $20 burden thrown upon him in some way or another. This simply drives up the cost of his loan to a fantastic height.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring in my little contribution to the debate on the bill proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I would like also to say a few words on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge). In my view that amendment could not have been better timed. This motion tends to refer this bill to the committee on banking and commerce, which would give us a chance to deal at the same time with other questions concerning Canadian economy and more especially the caisses populaires.
As a matter of fact, we all know that the caisses populaires are ready to render great services in the province of Quebec and, if we were given the opportunity to examine the steps required to improve their services, the bill introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia would not have to be debated each year.
The caisses populaires offer numerous advantages, since they grant loans for the building of houses, at a very reasonable rate. It would be very interesting for the members of the standing committee on banking and commerce to compare the advantages offered by the caisses populaires with those

offered by the banks. They would realize that the law is more favourable to the banks than to the caisses populaires, namely in the field of loans for house building. They would realize that loans granted by the banks for house building are guaranteed by the government, while those granted by the caisses are not. They would also realize that the loan terms required of the caisses populaires are accessible to a greater number of people, most particularly to that category of people who cannot afford the luxury of building homes in accordance with the requirements of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, the government grants a 15 per cent guaranty on loans granted by the banks for the building of houses, while it does not grant any on those granted by the caisses populaires.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, allow me to remind you that there is in the province of Quebec a rather awkward situation which is hard to explain.
People who build homes financed by the caisses populaires get a 3 per cent refund from the provincial government. However, persons who build with money loaned by banks do not get this rebate, for reasons of autonomy, it is claimed. This creates a situation about which we would have liked to hear some explanation from the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). Why does not the province of Quebec refund part of the interest paid by those who build houses whose plans have been approved by the inspectors of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation?
