Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to rise tonight to take part in this debate upon a subject about which I have thought much from time to time and which is of great interest to my constituents. Judging from the number of speeches on the bill so far today I would say it is a subject of common interest amongst all the members from whatever parts of the country they come.
The topic is more interesting perhaps than would be indicated by the shortness of the bill presented because one is able, by listening to the debate, to get some idea of the amount of worry involved in those simple little words dealing with the maximum amount of interest. Interest being, as it is, a part of our system of credit in this country and our system of credit playing the important part that it does in our national affairs, we have today heard representatives from most walks of life and we have covered most subjects that one would hear normally discussed in the budget debate. I expect that even more topics will be covered before the
Interest Act
debate is over. I certainly hope that more of my friends and colleagues will take part in this discussion and will reinforce me in my belief that this subject matter is one of great importance to all parts of Canada.
I do not pretend to be an expert on matters of interest and the economy, or on how best people should manage their affairs, but I have on occasion, as a lawyer in my private practice, attempted to help out some people who have been, shall we say, victimized by some of the abuses of our present credit system. I am not going to belabour our lending institutions entirely. I believe that this evening I may be guilty of saying the occasional harsh word about such institutions as the finance companies. However, I hope I shall be fair enough to give what I believe to be the case for their side as well.
I felt that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) who presented this bill was perhaps a little bit wild in some of his statements. For instance, he referred to the fantastic and exorbitant rates of interest that are paid by some people. He gave as an example a simple little transaction involving a small amount of credit by a large company and pointed that out as an example of a fantastic and exorbitant rate of interest. Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to flay my friend. However, I thought it was only fair-and I said I was going to try to be fair-to point out how I thought my friend was a trifle unfair, so that I may be more easily judged in that respect. I thought his remark with regard to that store must be admitted by any fair-minded person to be anything but fair.
In order to present the other side of the story, instead of saying that they had paid a fantastic rate of interest, I think he should also have said that those people had a charge account opened up for them on a minor purchase of $20; that the store was put to the expense probably of checking the credit rating of the person, of opening up an account in the person's name, of taking care of the bookkeeping entries, of providing the staff personnel to look after it, of making sure it was collected on time and took the risk of loss. Certainly for one isolated purchase, when the matter is looked at in that way, the individual purchaser has had $2.50 worth of services.
Certainly I would not want anyone to construe my words to mean that I am happy to see them pay even $2.50 for the services or that I am happy to see the amount of the service charge, compared to the amount of credit, bearing a somewhat disproportionate share of interest compared to the interest rates one would expect on a long term basis

Interest Act
when dealing with many purchases. However, what my hon. friend has done has, I think, opened up what should have been an enlightening part of this discussion.
There is such a thing as interest rates that are paid without any official charge. I am not talking about interest rates which are stated to be six per cent but are charged in advance, with no attention being paid to the final balance owing. Again I am not speaking of the various dodges by which storekeepers and others who lend money can sometimes fool purchasers or borrowers into feeling that they are not paying the rate of interest which they actually are paying. But it is a fact that, no matter what it may be called, whenever credit is extended for any purpose, inevitably one must pay interest. Certainly the storekeeper who buys his goods must do so. Whether he keeps them on the shelf for a long time and therefore has his money tied up and is paying the bank interest on that money or whether he sells them to a consumer who does not pay him for months, the fact remains that the storekeeper is always paying interest on the money that is owed. The money that is owed is an integral part of the price of each and every article that we use or come in contact with every day. I therefore suggest that one of the most important ways in which interest is passed along to the consumer is included in that vague term "price".
The bill that my hon. friend has introduced deals only with the most obvious and glaring examples where the interest rate is shown in the contract and where it is possible, without much imagination and without much digging, to find out exactly how much interest was paid. Obviously, if-as I believe to be the case-that interest appears really in the ordinary price without ever being called by that name it would be a simple step to have the extra interest included in the price. It is no secret today to any thinking person who has taken the trouble to examine today's marketing habits and who has gone from one store to the next to see how they are handling their merchandising to find that in fact a great many stores have discovered how unpopular interest is. They therefore make a big thing out of advertising to the effect that there are no carrying charges and no interest rates. I should be delighted if my hon. friend who introduced this bill would explain to us how this piece of legislation is going to protect the ordinary buyer of that type of merchandise.
I do not want to be misinterpreted. I am not saying that there is anything wrong with that type of merchandising. I am merely suggesting that the ordinary person does not

realize the amount of money he is actually paying for the use of money in the purchase price of every article. He might buy it on a long or a short term, but due to the merchandising practice of the firm from whom he buys in this instance their over-all charge for the use of the money is of necessity much higher than those who price their goods lower and add interest charges. In one instance the consumer himself can see how much interest is paid and the store can see the exact number of people who fall down, but in the other case it is certainly much harder for the ordinary person to detect.
I want to emphasize this point. I am not at all opposed to the principle of trying to protect people from excessive interest charges in certain respects at least. I feel that the idea of bringing in legislation to curb if possible the activities of the most vicious type of money lender we have in this country is a very sound one. I am merely suggesting that the present bill does not do what we should like to see it do. I am speaking against the terms of the bill itself; I am not speaking against the noble and ambitious idea of protecting members of the public against excessive rates of interest.
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to deal solely with what I call hidden finance charges in my little talk tonight. I merely digressed for a few minutes to mention it as one of the factors which has interested me throughout the whole debate; to such an extent, perhaps, that I have been unable to concentrate as much as I should on some of the speeches which have been made this afternoon. A wealth of information has been brought to light, and although some of it has, no doubt, been brought to the attention of the house before, I feel that in the main it is very sound. It has been most helpful, and since the subject we are discussing today is a very important one I hope I may be forgiven if by inadvertency I repeat anything which has already been said by another hon. member. I will try to be as original as I can but there has not been an original thinker for a long time and I do not pretend to have made the grade myself.
I am especially interested in one field of finance, namely the consumer finance field of automobile and truck financing. There are in Canada today a great number of companies which finance perhaps between 75 per cent and 90 per cent of all the vehicles on the road. My principal concern is not just with the working man who has had to finance a family car. It is true that many of them are paying a rate of interest for their money which they really cannot afford. They buy automobiles and for the amount of use they get out of them it would seem

it is rather harsh on them that they should have to pay such a relatively large sum of money by way of finance particularly since they use their cars only from time to time and mainly for pleasure. Many of these owners find at the end of a year or so that the car has cost them much more than they had calculated and yet they have gone badly into debt and paid large sums of money to the finance company. For this there is, after all, a very simple remedy. The vehicle is, after all, used only for pleasure. No one has forced the owner to buy it, and if the car becomes too expensive they are not obliged to finance it. Certainly these people are to a great extent the authors of their own misfortunes. We do not like the situation but we do not have to get really worried about it because the situation is one that can be avoided.
My concern is with the family breadwinner and a situation which often occurs in the trucking industry. A great many of the trucks on the highways today are financed by a finance company. The people who run these trucks have not to a great extent perhaps the background of experience necessary to enable them to judge all the factors, particularly the cost factors involved in operating a trucking business. To a great extent they have been dazzled by hearing of the amount of money that can be earned by hauling just one load from, say, Edmonton to Toronto and back. The income looks tremendous. So they go to a finance company and put down every cent they have in order to buy a truck. I suppose that here again it can be said that the trucker has, after all, made his own choice. He can invest his money in any way he likes in order to help earn a living. But the fact is that he does have to try to earn a living; he has a duty to his family, and should there be an error of judgment on his part it is one of the gestures made by a man who is not doing something merely for pleasure but risking every cent he has in trying to set himself up in business. It is certainly a very laudable objective for any working man to try to get out on his own and earn money on his own. That is what is at the heart of this economic system of ours and it is the spirit which we feel makes our way of life perhaps a little better than any other.
The trucker finds that he has to pay a much smaller down payment to the finance company than many people would think possible. It is quite possible for a man to get into the trucking business, where the combined value of a truck and trailer may run between $15,000 and $20,000, by putting down no more than $2,000 of his own cash. What the trucker fails to realize is that his profit
Interest Act
must take care of his finance charges, earn a living for himself and his family and provide enough to take care of the depreciation of the truck. This must all be done, really, out of his $2,000 investment.
He is operating a business with a $20,000 capital. Approximately $18,000 of that capital must earn profits of 15 to 20 per cent before he can break even. He fails to realize that in order to break even and before he can draw wages he must be operating a business which makes a clear profit of 10 to 15 per cent. Obviously many businessmen are quite happy to earn 10 or 15 per cent annually. My hon. friends in the C.C.F. group would feel they were being positively hoggish if they asked for anything more. I suggest that the practice of permitting the purchase of what is really a large and expensive business with such a small down payment is one of the worst faults I can find with finance companies today.
The effect is not just to make it difficult for that particular man to make a living. The effect is that automatically the trucking field becomes very crowded by people who for the most part should never have entered it in the first place because they do not understand the amount of financing required or what kind of profit they must make to break even. The situation soon develops in this field, as it would in any other field of small business, where it is crowded with bad businessmen and this plays havoc with the rates. It is most disturbing to what is at the best of times a difficult and highly competitive industry in which to operate.
The man who has invested his hard earned life savings as a down payment on a truck has no cash reserve on which to fall back. He is over-financed in so far as his total amount of borrowings is concerned but under-financed for going into business. He must, therefore, pay a set amount of money each month to the finance company and in order to do so he must keep working no matter what rate may obtain. Consequently if the prevailing rates are such that jobs are somewhat scarce he must quickly bid the rates down and in a period of slight recession trucking rates decline in a short space of time to about half the amount that is really necessary in order to pay the long term costs. Simply because the finance companies make it so easy to obtain money in this manner we find that an entire industry can be made most unstable with the result that an entire group of honest hardworking, conscientious truckers who have spent years and years to properly learn their business and to put it on a profitable businesslike basis can find themselves almost ruined by the actions of a small group with what I will call irresponsibly financed money.

Interest Act
I do not want to be mistaken in my argument in this regard. Certainly I can see the advantage to any small trucker. A truck driver who is able to save a few dollars and who feels it is worth the effort to go to a finance company and take whatever risks are involved or pay whatever rates of interest he feels he must in order to purchase his own truck and by hard work build up a small business of which he may be proud is free to do so. This again is an example of the pioneer, independent, democratic spirit we like and would not want to see crushed. I am not suggesting that before the finance company buys the paper from the man who sold the truck it should give the purchaser of the truck a complete test as to his finances nor am I suggesting that he should be given psychological tests to determine if he is competent to conduct a proper business. However, it is not too much to ask that the finance company at least check to see if the man really has the one requisite that is necessary before money is invested into a business. In other words they must determine if he knows anything about the business.
My hon. friends have been most patient. I have not mentioned the word "interest" for a while but I am sure I have made my point sufficiently clear. After all, when the truckers get in trouble and lose their trucks or when the trucks break down and they are unable to keep them in a proper state of repair it simply means that more of them go broke and losses are high. The incidence of loss is an extremely important factor in determining interest rates. Interest rates for the entire trucking industry are much too high in my opinion.
It is not just with respect to the automobile financing field that I have a few complaints. There is another large group of finance companies and these, for want of a better name, I will call the direct loan or personal loan companies. These companies are characterized by what has today become perhaps the universal tragedy. Their most popular slogan, come on, or gimmick is one designed to bring everyone into their office: "Come in and see us if you have financial troubles; if you cannot pay your debts come in and we will take care of them for you."
I confess, Mr. Speaker, when I hear of the number of people who fall for this line and who actually go to these finance companies I begin to wonder if my ordinary fellow citizens have the high degree of intelligence for which I have always given them credit. The fact is the direct loan companies play that tune to an extent which almost becomes nauseous and the effects are vicious. In order to get the finance companies to pay their debts people who are already in debt

must pay more interest on their debts and therefore they are really adding to the total debt by going to the company although they do not seem to realize this. In addition to that, if they are really influenced by this slogan they are so relieved that in an expansive mood they promptly walk down to the store that has just been paid off and, finding that their credit has been reinstated, buy more stuff that they cannot afford and should not purchase.
I have had it pointed out to me by people engaged in this field that the finance companies do provide a service to this type of debtor, that they do prevent the people from being hounded by other creditors and that, after all, the finance companies are entitled to a certain charge because they render a certain service. I do not quarrel with that but I regret that the type of advertisement the companies employ which seems so successful attracts the person who is already in financial difficulty. The companies appear to take the attitude that this group of people is their special meat and I feel they should draw the line somewhere.
I do not wish to extend my remarks unduly but if hon. members will bear with me I will touch lightly upon a few more facts. When we are attempting to decide how to amend the existing legislation in this field we must ask ourselves if it will do the job we want it to. We should pause and examine to see just how much needs to be done. For instance, if I am correct in interpreting the motive that would impel an hon. member to bring in a bill such as this it would appear that we are conscious of a need to protect people from exorbitant rates of interest.
Since we are discussing a bill designed to protect people, we should see just how much protection they already have. There are a tremendous number of acts in force in the various provinces which do hedge in the ordinary citizen. They support him on the left hand and on the right hand and protect him from getting into a lot of trouble. For instance, dealings with finance companies with respect to motor cars were mentioned. I think I mentioned it-if I did not I apologize but it can stand being mentioned twice-that in Alberta we have the conditional sales act which protects the purchaser from having to pay off the balance of what he owes on a car after he has lost the vehicle. Interest charges are limited as well by the Bank Act, the Small Loans Act and the Bankruptcy Act, and there is legislation protecting mortgage holders, and so forth.
Now, the general effect of all these acts is that we are in fact restricting in an ever narrowing degree the necessity of an

ordinary citizen thinking for himself or taking care of himself. I can recall the phrase that I have heard for years, namely, caveat emptor. I think that the mere mention of this phrase today is enough to cause most of my hon. friends to scream in anguish because we have gone so far away from it. Certainly, there must be a limit beyond which we must not mollycoddle grown-up citizens. Are we so ashamed of their will power that we want to protect them from any indiscretion whatsoever? Do we feel that they are so weak-kneed, so uneducated, so misdirected in their dealings with their fellow men and in their handling of their own businesses that we want to lead them by the hand at every age through life? I suggest, that that is not the way to build citizens who have strength of character, will power and the know-how to make leaders of the Canadian people, because our people are the raw materials which will advance and make this country of ours even greater than it has been. I am therefore, in one respect at least opposed to the thinking behind this bill. I am opposed to it because I feel it is unduly restricting the activities of our citizens.
I would not want to condemn any member for wanting to protect them and certainly these are two important factors. I feel that I have been perhaps a little too long on these two simple points, but if the house will bear with me I have one more point I should like to make. It has been mentioned today that interest rates are part of the price of money. When we consider the means of protecting people from wasting their money by paying the present interest charges and so forth, we should remember that the lending of money is a business. The money itself is the product of that business. If we decide that we must put a ceiling on interest rates, then we are automatically putting a ceiling on the possibility of profit in any money transactions.
In this country a person has the right to invest his money in any business he likes, whether he is in the construction business or in any other business. Certainly, I think it is unfair and discriminatory to put a ceiling on interest rates, as is suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia. We should be very careful before we discriminate against any one class because if we do we say to him, "Your investment is of the type that we do not like and therefore we will not allow you to make as much profit as we will allow a man to make who had the foresight to put his money into a brickyard." Certainly, we must not have discrimination of that kind. I think that even
Interest Act
my hon. friends on the other side of the house would not really press this too hard if they realized that they were in fact trying to discriminate against one group of profitmaking citizens in this country.
I notice signs of movement in the house, Mr. Speaker. The remarks that I said would take a few minutes have stretched overly long.
I hope that on the next occasion a bill similar to this comes up I shall be able to speak on a few other points similar to those which I have made which I think hon. members might find interesting.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in rising to take part in this debate because in my constituency, as in most other constituencies in Canada today, there are a great many good, solid citizens and a lot of young folk who are taking advantage of instalment buying and the procurement of credit to make for themselves a good standard of living. Like other hon. members who have spoken, I have been very much impressed by the frank and sincere manner in which this debate has taken place today. I was very much impressed this afternoon by the way in which the bill was introduced. I was impressed by the thinking behind the moving of the amendment which suggested that the subject matter of this bill be given further study and it is my feeling that that is what should happen to the subject matter of the bill.
Today we have heard a great deal of terminology such as fantastic interest rates, the exploiting of the people, loan sharks, exorbitant interest rates, and so on. All of these words did create word pictures which perhaps did not follow the judgment and the thinking of the members concerned. With your permission, sir, just for a few moments, I should like to deal as frankly and as simply as I can with the elements of this matter and try to see what we as ordinary people would derive from the passage of this bill. I think perhaps I and most people do resent the fact that the borrowers of money have been represented here as something in the manner of weak-kneed people who fall prey to every person who has money to lend, regardless of the terms involved. I do not think that is a common practice at all. I think perhaps that when you are in need of money you shop around for the lowest interest rate, and I think most people shop around in this way as they shop for everything else.
We have heard today of various cases of extremely high interest rates and I am sure there must be such cases of extreme rates of interest charged. I wonder how many of these cases there are compared with the very many

Interest Act
thousands of cases of people in dire necessity who obtain money and are very thankful for it, as it aids them in their time of distress.
We appreciate that in this day and age everyone wants the most for the least, and certainly no one wants to pay a high rate of interest if a lower rate can be procured. We have heard today of the large stores with varying interest rates from 12 per cent to 54 per cent. The names of Eaton's and Simp-sons-Sears were mentioned. I wonder whether this is a true picture of what actually happens. I should like to take as an example a boat with a purchase price of $1,800 that one might purchase from one of these stores on a monthly payment basis, with the interest and carrying charges included in the monthly instalments. I am sure if you will look at the matter very carefully, as most prospective shoppers do, you will find that the total price of the boat paid for on the instalment basis will be just about the same as the cash purchase price in the store next door. I suggest that this may be the case because corporations as large as Simpsons-Sears or Eaton's by making volume purchases can buy these boats at a price that makes this possible. So, perhaps this is a service to the public rather than a case of an extremely high rate of interest.
An interest rate of 12 per cent has been suggested today as the maximum amount that should be payable. I am not sure that this would be a workable percentage. Nothing was put before us today about the mechanics of such a maximum rate. We are not assured that a 12 per cent interest rate would be feasible and that the agencies lending money today could operate with a rate of 12 per cent. We are asked to assume that they can.
It is true that there are credit unions operating today at a 12 per cent interest rate. May I point out that perhaps they can do this because they do not have the expenses that other lending agencies have. We know of some instances where they do not have to pay for accommodation. There are instances where the people who operate credit unions do so on a voluntary basis. They certainly do not spend the same amount of money in advertising because in most cases their advertising is done by word of mouth or in leaflet form. There is not the extreme type of advertising that was illustrated this afternoon. Therefore they can perhaps operate at a 12 per cent limit whereas it would be impossible in most other instances. May I point out that although credit unions do operate most successfully one will still find that some of the members of various credit unions do take advantage of other sources of credit even though they have available the privileges of the credit union.
[Mr. Danforth.l
We have not heard anything today about the point of view of the lending agencies with regard to the matter of the limiting of interest rates. Where they are so directly concerned I suggest that it would perhaps be feasible to bring them into the discussion in order to present their views in full because I am sure they do not like the publicity that goes with extreme interest rates. It does not help their business a bit to have these cases widely publicized, and such cases are the ones that are widely publicized. I am sure that they would have as much interest as anyone else in seeing that such a situation did not exist and that proper legislation was brought forward to prevent its happening.
I wonder whether the legitimate lending companies do make the extreme amounts that have been portrayed today. If their profits are so high I wonder why there is not a rush to get into the legistimate business of lending money in this way. The numbers of loan companies do not vary to that extent. I should like to quote a paragraph from a speech containing reference to a brief submitted by the Canadian consumer loan association to the banking and commerce committee in 1956, which reads as follows:
They compare profits, before deducting interest on borrowed money and income taxes, expressed as a percentage of employed assets, as between the consumer loan industry and 66 companies representing a cross section of Canadian industry. Included are such industries as utilities, steel, foodstuffs, newsprint, petroleum and base metals. It was found that consumer loan company profits for 1954 adjusted for the rates now in force ranged from 5i per cent to 91 per cent. Profits of the other companies ranged from 61 per cent to 27 per cent and averaged out to 17 per cent.
I wonder whether these loan companies do charge the high rates of interest that have been portrayed. Today we have heard, even though a 12 per cent rate of interest has been suggested, that perhaps this rate could be too high. I am sure that everyone is interested in as low a rate of interest as possible and if everybody was assured that a 12 per cent rate would result in enough capital being placed on the market for creditors to borrow I am sure everybody would be happy with the situation. But there is always the danger that if the interest rate is limited the necessary capital will not be there.
I wonder what would happen to the people if they were not able to borrow the money they need. I have here a booklet entitled, "Three Experiments with Small Loan Interest Rates", reprinted from the Harvard Business Review, in which it is stated that in the state of New Jersey legislation was passed reducing interest rates from 3 per cent to 1J per cent a month. This article deals with what actually does take place when

interest rates are reduced by legislation. I should like to read briefly from the booklet to indicate what did happen in the state of New Jersey.
When the rate reduction bill was passed in May, 1929, the volume of loans outstanding exceeded $20 million; on November 30, 1931, the volume was $5,400,000. The number of licensees declined from 437 on November 30, 1928, to 117 on November 30, 1931.
Chattel loans were reduced from $16,700,000 on November 30, 1928, to $3,400,000 on November 30, 1931, a three-year period. The article goes on to state:
Of the $3,400,000 of chattel loans outstanding on November 30,	1931, approximately $600,000 was
reported by licensees who were making no new loans, and approximately $2,400,000 was reported by the eight offices of the Household Finance Corporation. This company, which had voluntarily reduced its monthly interest rate to 21 per cent in 1928, announced that it could not operate profitably at li per cent a month.
In 1932, after three years of the 1J per cent rate, the New Jersey legislature increased the maximum rate of interest on small loans to 2J per cent a month. I merely bring this to your attention to show that such a thing is possible. It is possible for us to legislate ourselves out of very necessary money.
I should like to put the thought before the house that perhaps those who borrow money are perfectly aware of the interest rates, that they know they are paying more than they would in other cases but feel that their investment is such that they are willing to take the chance in accepting this greater financial burden because they believe it will be a good investment. May I point out that perhaps this extra money would make possible the purchase of the farm next door which perhaps would not be on the market again for a generation, so the necessary money would have to be procured at once and perhaps the size of the necessary loan would not make it possible to borrow from the bank. May I point out that perhaps a fisherman is buying a new car, and suddenly has the opportunity of buying a share in the fishing boat he is operating. Perhaps he needs this source of credit to buy the share which was allotted to him.
There could be the possibility that the home down the street would suddenly be for sale, the one that the gentleman in question wished to buy and perhaps change into an apartment building as an additional source of income. There are many instances in which this capital is necessary, and I am sure those who borrow it are very certain of the interest rates they are obliged to pay and are very willing to pay them.
Interest Act
I have stated before that I am sure every hon. member in this house and the constituents they represent wish to have the opportunity of borrowing money at the lowest possible rate of interest. People do think of their pocketbooks. The bill, as it has been presented, would go a long way in limiting the amount of interest that could be charged. But I wonder if enough thought has been given to the 12 per cent rate. We have no idea whether it should be 12 per cent, 15 per cent or even 20 per cent. We are given 12 per cent as being, in effect, the ideal. I am suggesting that support should be given to the amendment so that the subject matter could be referred to the committee for further study and investigation. We all know that there are circumstances in which exorbitant rates of interest are being charged. These are the ones that we wish to legislate against, not the legitimate businesses that are trying to do a fine job. I am sure that if the officials of these companies were called in for consultation they would offer sound advice as to how such police measures could be introduced.

speechtext: I rise at this late hour, Mr. Speaker, in these proceedings to take part in this very interesting debate. I should like to compliment the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) upon the very energetic and sincere manner in which he has introduced this bill. I would think that if the members of his party were in full accord with this bill they would lend more support to him than they have today.

speechtext: We do not want to talk it out; we want a vote.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I think there are only two members in that corner who have taken part in the debate and brought some of these facts to our attention. I feel there are many more complex aspects of this bill than those which are being brought before us by the sponsor of the bill or the other members of his party.
I do not think there is any doubt about the importance of credit. We have all heard this afternoon and this evening about the many important phases of credit in so far as our economic structure is concerned. This has been very forcibly brought to our attention by many of the previous speakers. Since we have changed from an agrarian civilization to a more or less industrial civilization, a change has been brought about in our attitude toward this matter of credit. The suburban type of life that many live today has created a need for credit. The great increase in the volume of money lent by these companies is proof without a doubt of the need for this business of lending money. If it were otherwise I think we would not have seen the great expansion that we have seen in this business.

Interest Act
The government has kept pretty well apace with this expanding business in so far as legislation is concerned. I should like to bring to the attention of the house the various implications of the dovetailing of these two bills, No. C-3 and No. C-5, the amendment to Small Loans Act and the amendment to the Interest Act. I feel they are very closely related. Up until the Small Loans Act was passed in 1939 the only applicable law was the Money-Lenders Act which restricted the rate of interest on loans up to $500 to 12 per cent per annum. No mention was made in that act of the interest rate that might be charged on larger loans and this created a problem which resulted in interest rates of 400 per cent or 500 per cent developing. The Small Loans Act, therefore, was designed to plug the gap by providing for a rate, including all charges of any kind, on loans up to $500.
After a long study in which many interesting witnesses were called from social welfare groups, banks and loan companies, and after discussing it very thoroughly the committee decided that two per cent per month on the unpaid balance was a fair and reasonable rate. However, there was no restriction on loans over $500 until 1956, only three years ago. It was apparent at that time that the Small Loans Act needed overhauling. As a result we have, as you know, rates of interest set at 2 per cent per month on the unpaid balance up to $300; one per cent from $300 to $1,000, and one-half of one per cent from $1,000 to $1,500. Briefly, that is the government's position with regard to the legislation which is in force to protect borrowers in Canada. I feel, Mr. Speaker, this is as far as we should go. It takes care of by far the largest group of borrowers. It takes care of the group that we wish to protect just as much as our friends in the C.C.F. wish to protect them. I feel the low income group is protected by the Small Loans Act today.
Another point I feel we should consider before any changes are made is that this lending business is a process whereby money is bought and sold on the lending market. We all know that the cost of buying money is higher today than it was a while ago. I believe, in fairness to the loan companies, we should mention the fact that their costs of operation have gone up as well. I believe, therefore, it would be improper at this time to make a change, for that reason alone. After all, we should not be asked to legislate to protect people against their lack of good judgment or common sense. I do not believe it is practical to legislate to cover all situations in which people may find themselves. I understood the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) to say that in his

province there was a ceiling imposed on the rate of interest that credit unions could charge. I wonder why the family he mentioned did not go to one of the credit unions to borrow the money because in this way they would have been protected to the same extent this bill suggests we should protect them. I should like to hear more of the facts in that particular case, because it seems rather odd to me that a well established bank would turn down a request for a $2,400 loan when the applicant had a house which was completely paid for and had no encumbrance against it.
The hon. member for Assiniboia told the house this afternoon that the total of all consumer credit outstanding in Canada, as of September, 1958 was $1,947 million, according to the Bank of Canada statistics survey from which he quoted. He also went on to say that, according to that same survey, the banks had done a poor job on the consumer credit basis. He went on to say that they had been doing only about 25 per cent of the consumer credit business. But that business in total is $499 million. This amount of business done by the banks was transacted on the basis of approximately Ilf per cent, or about the same figure that he is proposing in this bill. Of this total amount of business of $1,947 million, the small loans companies did $372 million worth. That is a terrific amount of business which they have done, over and above what the banks have done. These people that use the small loans companies which had this vast amount of business went to those loans companies for various reasons. Maybe their credit rating was not sufficient for the banks; maybe it was a matter of accessibility; maybe some personal reasons were involved. There may have been many reasons why they went to the small loans companies and did $372 million worth of business.
If my hon. friend wishes to take away this opportunity and to make this amount of money unavailable to the people of Canada, where will these people go for their credit? What effect will this action have on our country's economic situation? I have heard hon. members talking, not only in that corner of the house but in other places, about unemployment. If we take $372 million out of circulation on the small loans companies basis, I would think that action would have a direct bearing on unemployment today. What about those thousands of young people who are moving into new homes? How are they going to furnish these homes and equip them with stoves, refrigerators, and such things if small loans are not made available to them?

Business of the House
Then I come to this business of 54 per cent interest on a $20 article which the hon. member mentioned this afternoon. I am not going to say anything about the 54 per cent. I am going to stick to that figure of $2.25 which he used in respect of this particular article. It might be a hot plate; it might be a steam kettle or some other appliance or piece of equipment which is needed. The buyer of this piece of equipment may feel, "It is worth $2.25 to me to have this piece of equipment; we need it and in order to increase our standard of living it is essential". He is therefore quite willing to pay $2.25 for the use of this article. I do not think it is the function of the government to tell that man whether he should or should not have this article, or whether it is essential that he have this product. I do not see why we should be asked to legislate in order to alter people's minds. We must give people some credit for using common sense and good judgment.
There is another way in which to look at this matter. Maybe this particular article was on sale. Maybe he saved two or three dollars by buying it when it was on sale and so saved the $2.25 or at least had that saving coming to him as a result of this special sale. I think there are many occasions when it may be advantageous to the purchaser to use the small loans business which is made available to him. It may be all right for us to pass legislation whereby we tell the lenders that they cannot charge more than 12 per cent for loans. But on the other hand, we cannot tell them that they must lend the money. That is a decision that it is up to the businessman to make, in my opinion. This would not be the case if the socialistic idea were put into force.
This bill would freeze the limit of interest on credit to 12 per cent. On the one hand you would freeze the interest rate on the money lent. But on the other hand, the loan companies must go out and buy the money. On the one hand they are told they cannot charge more than 12 per cent. On the other hand, there is nothing in the act to say that
the price at which they buy this money must be a stable one. You cannot freeze the rate on one side without doing the same thing on the other side. The selling price and the cost price of money must be handled in the same way in either case.
I take the view, Mr. Speaker, that we are operating under a free enterprise system. I am happy to say that I belong to a party which down through the years has promoted free enterprise in business. I feel that money is no different from any other commodity; it is bought and it is sold. In a free market it will seek its own level. If this business of small loans is as lucrative as our friends in the corner tell us it is, I say that many people will get into the small loans business. The more people we get into the small loans business, the more competitive it will become and in the long run competition should control the maximum and control the business. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel that at the present time the situation is well in hand.
